subject: Linux & Shell for DevOps
summary: Linux is the substrate every other DevOps tool sits on: a container is a Linux process with namespaced views and cgroup limits, a Kubernetes node is a Linux box, and a CI runner is a shell script that will do exactly what you literally typed. This subject covers the kernel-level mechanisms an SRE is expected to reason about - inodes and file descriptors, the permission and capability model, process lifecycle and signals, systemd's dependency graph and cgroups, memory reclaim and the OOM killer - alongside the operational toolkit for triaging a machine you have never seen before at three in the morning. Interviewers probe it because it is where surface knowledge collapses: anyone can recite that chmod 777 fixes permissions, but only someone who has actually operated systems can explain why df and du disagree, why a container ignores SIGTERM, or why the load average is 40 while the CPU is idle.

sections.title: 1. One Tree, Many Devices: The Filesystem Hierarchy
sections.content:
Linux has no drive letters. There is exactly one namespace, rooted at `/`, and every storage device, network share, and kernel-generated pseudo-filesystem is grafted into it at a mount point. `/dev/nvme0n1p2` is not a location you can `cd` into; it becomes reachable only once you mount it somewhere, and whatever directory you mount it on temporarily hides whatever was already in that directory. That single fact causes a surprising number of production incidents, which we will come back to.

The layout itself follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, and the standard is worth understanding as a set of intentions rather than a list to memorise. The organising question is: who owns this data, how often does it change, and does it need to survive a reboot?

`/usr` holds everything the package manager installs: binaries, libraries, shared data, documentation. On any modern distribution `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/lib` and `/lib64` are just symlinks into `/usr/bin` and `/usr/lib` (the "usr-merge"). The original split existed because `/` had to be small enough to boot from while `/usr` might live on a separate, later-mounted disk. Initramfs made that obsolete: the kernel now unpacks a temporary root into RAM containing everything needed to find and mount the real root, so the early-boot argument for splitting binaries disappeared. The payoff of the merge is that `/usr` can be a single, self-contained, even read-only image — which is exactly how immutable and container-oriented distributions ship.

`/etc` is host-specific configuration: text files, no binaries, small, and the single most valuable thing to back up on a hand-built machine. `/var` is variable state that grows at runtime — logs in `/var/log`, package databases and application state in `/var/lib` (this includes `/var/lib/docker` and `/var/lib/containerd`, which is why `/var` is usually the first filesystem to fill on a container host), spool directories in `/var/spool`. `/run` is a tmpfs, wiped on every boot, holding PID files and unix sockets; it replaced `/var/run`, which survives as a compatibility symlink. `/tmp` is world-writable with the sticky bit set and is frequently a tmpfs too, meaning files written there consume RAM and vanish on reboot. `/opt` is for self-contained third-party software that does not follow the hierarchy; `/usr/local` is for software you installed outside the package manager, and the package manager must never touch it. `/boot` holds the kernel and initramfs and is often a small separate partition — which is why "apt upgrade fails, no space left on device" is so often really "`/boot` is full of five old kernels".

Three directories are not on any disk at all. `/proc` is procfs, a kernel interface dressed as files: one numbered directory per running process plus system-wide entries like `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/self/mounts`. `/sys` is sysfs, the device model and its tunables — this is where you read a NIC's link speed or a disk's I/O scheduler. `/dev` is devtmpfs, populated by the kernel and managed by udev. Reading `/proc/loadavg` is not reading a file; it is a syscall wearing a costume, which is why these entries report size 0 and cannot be usefully copied around.

The production failure this section is really about is mounting over a non-empty directory. If an application writes 40 GB into `/var/lib/mysql` while the intended data disk is not mounted, and someone later mounts the disk there, those 40 GB are still on the root filesystem, still consuming space, and completely invisible to `du` because the mount shadows them. `df` shows the space used; `du` cannot find it. The fix is to bind-mount the real root somewhere else and look underneath.
sections.code:
# The mount table is ground truth, not /etc/fstab (which is only intent).
findmnt -t ext4,xfs,tmpfs        # tree view of what is actually mounted
cat /proc/self/mounts            # kernel's own view; /etc/mtab is a symlink to this

# What filesystem is this path on, and where is its mount point?
df -hT /var/lib/docker
findmnt -no SOURCE,FSTYPE,OPTIONS --target /var/lib/docker

# Space used but invisible to du -> something is hidden UNDER a mount point.
mkdir /mnt/root-underlay
mount --bind / /mnt/root-underlay          # the real root, ignoring mounts stacked on top
du -xhd1 /mnt/root-underlay/var/lib        # now the shadowed files are visible
umount /mnt/root-underlay

# Pseudo-filesystems: size 0, real content.
ls -l /proc/meminfo                        # -r--r--r-- 1 root root 0 ...
head -3 /proc/meminfo
cat /sys/class/net/eth0/speed              # 1000  (Mbit/s, straight from the driver)
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler         # [mq-deadline] kyber bfq none

sections.title: 2. Everything Is a File: Inodes, Links, and File Descriptors
sections.content:
A filename is not a file. On a Unix filesystem the file itself is an inode: a fixed-size structure holding metadata (type, permission bits, owner UID/GID, size, timestamps, link count) plus pointers to the data blocks. What the inode does *not* contain is the name. Names live in directories, and a directory is just a special file containing a list of (name, inode number) pairs. `ls -i` shows the number; `stat` shows everything else.

Once you internalise that, hard links stop being mysterious. `ln target newname` adds a second directory entry pointing at the same inode and increments the inode's link count. There is no "original" and no "copy" — the two names are peers, and removing either one merely decrements the count. The data is freed only when the count reaches zero. Because inode numbers are unique only within a filesystem, hard links cannot cross filesystems, and the kernel refuses hard links to directories because they would create cycles that `find` and `fsck` could not reason about. A symbolic link, by contrast, is its own inode whose contents are a path string. It can cross filesystems, can point at something that does not exist yet, and is resolved on every access — so if you move the target, the symlink silently breaks. `ls -l` shows a symlink as mode `lrwxrwxrwx`; the permission bits on a symlink are meaningless on Linux, because the target's permissions are what get checked.

Now the second half of "everything is a file": file descriptors. When a process opens something, the kernel returns a small non-negative integer that indexes into that process's descriptor table. Descriptor 0 is stdin, 1 is stdout, 2 is stderr by convention. Each descriptor points at an *open file description* holding the current offset and flags, which in turn points at the inode. That layering explains behaviours people find surprising: `dup2` makes two descriptors share one offset, which is exactly how shell redirection works, whereas two separate `open()` calls on the same file get independent offsets.

The link count is the mechanism behind the single most-asked Linux debugging question. `rm` does not delete data; it calls `unlink()`, which removes a directory entry. If a process still holds an open descriptor on that inode, the kernel keeps an internal reference, so a link count of zero is not enough — the blocks are freed only when the last descriptor closes. Delete a 100 GB log that nginx has open and the name disappears from `ls`, `du` can no longer see it, but `df` still reports the space as used. It comes back when the process is restarted or signalled to reopen its logs, or immediately if you truncate the file through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`. Every running process's descriptors are visible there as symlinks, which makes `/proc` the best forensic tool on the box: you can see exactly which files, sockets and pipes a process holds, and even read a config file that was deleted after startup.

One more consequence: inodes are a finite resource. ext4 allocates its inode table at `mkfs` time and cannot grow it, so a filesystem full of tiny files can report `No space left on device` while `df -h` shows 60% free — because `df -i` is at 100%. XFS allocates inodes dynamically and is far less prone to this, which is one practical reason it is the default on RHEL-family systems.

# Name vs inode
$ echo hello > a.txt
$ ln a.txt b.txt              # hard link: same inode, link count becomes 2
$ ln -s a.txt c.txt           # symlink: new inode whose content is the string "a.txt"
$ ls -li
131074 -rw-r--r-- 2 dev dev  6 Mar  3 10:00 a.txt
131074 -rw-r--r-- 2 dev dev  6 Mar  3 10:00 b.txt
131075 lrwxrwxrwx 1 dev dev  5 Mar  3 10:00 c.txt -> a.txt
$ rm a.txt                    # b.txt still works (count -> 1); c.txt is now dangling

# The deleted-but-open file: df and du disagree
$ df -h /var        # 96% used
$ du -sh /var       # 12G   <-- 40G unaccounted for
$ lsof -nP +L1      # +L1 = link count < 1, i.e. unlinked but still open
COMMAND   PID  USER  FD  TYPE DEVICE   SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
nginx    1421  root   5w  REG  259,1 43112038400     0  982 /var/log/nginx/access.log (deleted)

# Two fixes. Preferred: make the process reopen its files.
kill -USR1 1421                       # nginx: reopen logs
# Emergency (space back instantly, process keeps running, that file's data is lost):
truncate -s 0 /proc/1421/fd/5

# Inode exhaustion looks like a full disk but isn't
df -h / ; df -i /
find /var -xdev -printf '%h\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head   # where the file swarm is

sections.title: 3. Permissions: rwx, Octal, and Why Directories Are Different
sections.content:
Every inode carries an owner UID, a group GID, and twelve permission bits. Nine of them are the familiar three triads — owner, group, other — each with read, write, execute. The kernel's check short-circuits, and this is the part candidates get wrong: it picks *exactly one* triad. If your UID matches the owner, the owner bits decide, full stop; the group and other bits are never consulted even when they are more permissive. So a file with mode `0477` owned by you is readable by you and by everyone else, but *not writable* by you even though "other" has write. This is occasionally used deliberately, and it is a good question for checking whether someone understands the algorithm rather than pattern-matching on `rwxr-xr-x`.

Octal is just the bit pattern: r=4, w=2, x=1 per triad. `644` is `rw-r--r--`, `755` is `rwxr-xr-x`, `600` is owner-only, `640` is the standard for a secret readable by one service group. Learn to read both directions instantly, because an interviewer will say "make the key 600 and the directory 750" and expect no calculator.

The meanings shift for directories, and that is where the real understanding lives. On a directory, `r` means you can *list* the names inside. `w` means you can create, rename, and delete entries — note that deleting a file is a write to its *directory*, not to the file, which is why you can delete a file you cannot read, and why the sticky bit had to be invented. And `x`, the search or traverse bit, means you can resolve a path *through* the directory to reach something inside. Traversal is what you almost always actually need: to read `/srv/app/config.yml` the kernel needs `x` on `/`, on `/srv`, and on `/srv/app`, plus `r` on the file itself. This yields two clean tricks. A directory with mode `0711` lets anyone open a file inside it if they already know the exact name, while nobody can enumerate the contents — which is why home directories are often `0711`. And a directory with `r--` lets you `ls` it but every `stat` fails, so `ls -l` shows names decorated with question marks.

The write-permission-lives-on-the-directory rule is also behind a common bug: you `chmod 400` a config file to "protect" it, but the deploy user still has write on the containing directory, so it can simply delete and recreate the file. Permissions on a file do not protect it from someone who controls its parent.

Ownership has its own rules. Only root can `chown` a file to a different user; otherwise you could dodge disk quotas or hand off a setuid binary. A non-root owner can `chgrp` a file, but only to a group they belong to. `chmod -R` is a classic source of outages: recursively setting `755` makes every private key and data file world-readable, and recursively setting `644` strips the traverse bit from directories and makes the whole tree unusable. The correct recursive idiom uses capital `X`, which sets execute only on directories and on files that already had at least one execute bit: `chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX dir`. And `chmod 777` is never the answer; it is what people type when they have not worked out which of the three access checks is actually failing.
sections.code:
# Reading modes
-rw-r-----  1 app appsecrets  640   owner rw, group r, world nothing
drwxr-x---  2 app app         750   owner full, group list+traverse, world nothing
-rwsr-xr-x  1 root root      4755   setuid root (see next section)

# Traverse-only directory: files readable if you know the name, contents not listable
$ chmod 711 /srv/keys
$ sudo -u nobody ls /srv/keys              # Permission denied
$ sudo -u nobody cat /srv/keys/known.pem   # works

# Safe recursive fix: X adds +x to directories only (and to already-executable files)
chmod -R u=rwX,go=rX /srv/app

# Or split it explicitly - clearer, and what belongs in a runbook
find /srv/app -type d -exec chmod 750 {} +
find /srv/app -type f -exec chmod 640 {} +

# Which path component is actually denying you? namei walks it and prints each mode.
$ namei -l /srv/app/config.yml
f: /srv/app/config.yml
drwxr-xr-x root root /
drwxr-x--- root root srv        <-- not root, not in root's group: denied right here
drwxr-x--- app  app  app
-rw-r----- app  app  config.yml

# Deleting depends on the directory, not the file
$ chmod 000 doomed.txt && rm doomed.txt    # rm prompts, but succeeds: you have w on the dir

sections.title: 4. setuid, setgid, the Sticky Bit, umask, and Capabilities
sections.content:
Above the nine rwx bits sit three more: setuid (octal 4000), setgid (2000), and the sticky bit (1000). They exist because Unix needed a way to let an unprivileged user perform a privileged action without becoming privileged in general.

A setuid binary runs with the effective UID of the file's *owner* rather than the caller's. The canonical example is `/usr/bin/passwd`: it is owned by root and setuid, so when an ordinary user runs it the process gains root's effective UID and can update `/etc/shadow`, a file the user cannot even read. `ls -l` shows this as `s` in the owner execute position (`-rwsr-xr-x`); a capital `S` means the setuid bit is set while the execute bit is not, which is nearly always a mistake. setgid does the same thing for the group.

setuid is the most dangerous bit in the model, because every setuid-root binary is a privilege escalation waiting for a bug: the attacker fully controls the argv, environment, resource limits, inherited file descriptors, and working directory of a process that is about to become root. Historic escapes came from `LD_PRELOAD` (the dynamic loader now ignores it for setuid binaries), from overflows in argument parsing, and from binaries that shell out. Two facts worth stating in an interview: the Linux kernel *ignores* the setuid bit on interpreted scripts — the unavoidable race between opening the script and the interpreter re-opening it made it unfixable, so `chmod u+s script.sh` does literally nothing — and mounting a filesystem `nosuid` disables the bit entirely, which is standard hardening for `/tmp`, `/home`, and removable media.

setgid on a *directory* means something different and genuinely useful: new files created inside inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group, and new subdirectories inherit the setgid bit itself. That is how you build a shared project tree where everyone's files automatically land in the `dev` group.

The sticky bit on a directory (`chmod +t`, giving `/tmp` its mode `1777`) restricts deletion: even though the directory is world-writable, you may only remove or rename entries you own. Without it any user could delete — or worse, replace — another user's temp files, which is the classic symlink-attack vector.

`umask` controls permissions at creation time. It is a mask of bits to *remove*. The kernel gives a new regular file mode `0666` and a new directory `0777`, then clears whatever the umask specifies. With the common default `022` you get `644` files and `755` directories; with `027` you get `640` and `750`, which is what you want on a multi-tenant server; with `077`, owner-only. Note that files never receive the execute bit at creation — compilers and `install` set it explicitly afterwards. umask is a per-process attribute inherited across `fork`, so setting it in your interactive shell affects only that shell's descendants. This is why the right place to set it for a daemon is the service manager: systemd has a `UMask=` directive and defaults to `0022`. A frequent production bug is a cron job or service writing files with the wrong mode because nobody set a umask there and the `/etc/profile` value never applied.

Finally, modern Linux offers a much sharper tool than setuid: capabilities. Root's power is split into distinct privileges — `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` (bind ports below 1024), `CAP_NET_RAW` (raw sockets, what `ping` needs), `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` (an unfortunate catch-all), `CAP_CHOWN`, and roughly forty others. You can grant a single capability to a binary with `setcap`, or better, to a service with systemd's `AmbientCapabilities=`, so the process never holds full root. `ping` on modern distributions is no longer setuid-root; it carries `cap_net_raw`. When an interviewer asks how to let a Java app listen on 443 without running as root, the strong answers are a capability, a high port plus a firewall redirect, or a reverse proxy — never `sudo java`.
sections.code:
# setuid in the wild
$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd /usr/bin/ping
-rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 68208 /usr/bin/passwd            # setuid root
-rwxr-xr-x 1 root root 76672 /usr/bin/ping              # NOT setuid any more...
$ getcap /usr/bin/ping
/usr/bin/ping cap_net_raw=ep                            # ...it carries one capability

# Audit every setuid/setgid binary (do this; unexpected entries are real findings)
find / -xdev -perm /6000 -type f -printf '%M %u %p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort

# Shared project directory: setgid so group ownership is inherited
chgrp dev /srv/project && chmod 2775 /srv/project
# Sticky bit: world-writable, but you can only delete your own entries
$ ls -ld /tmp
drwxrwxrwt 18 root root 4096 /tmp

# umask arithmetic
$ umask            # 0022
$ touch f && mkdir d && stat -c '%a %n' f d
644 f
755 d
$ umask 027 && touch g && mkdir e && stat -c '%a %n' g e
640 g
750 e

# Grant one capability instead of root (systemd drop-in)
[Service]
User=app
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes
UMask=0027

sections.title: 5. Processes: fork, exec, PIDs, and /proc
sections.content:
Unix creates processes with a pair of syscalls that at first looks redundant. `fork()` clones the calling process: the child receives a copy of the address space, the open file descriptors, the environment, the working directory and the signal dispositions, differing only in its PID and in `fork()`'s return value (0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent). `execve()` then discards the program the child is running and replaces it in place with a new binary, keeping the PID and, by default, the open descriptors. The copy is not a real copy — the kernel maps the parent's pages copy-on-write and duplicates a page only when someone writes to it — so forking a 4 GB process is cheap until it isn't.

The reason for the split is the gap between the two calls. Everything the shell does to set up a child happens in that window, in the child, after `fork` and before `exec`: redirect stdout by `dup2`-ing a file onto descriptor 1, drop privileges with `setuid`, change directory, set resource limits, close descriptors. If process creation were a single atomic "spawn program with these settings" call, every one of those knobs would have to be a parameter. This is precisely what happens when you type `ls > out.txt`: bash forks, the child opens `out.txt`, `dup2`s it onto fd 1, then execs `/usr/bin/ls`, which writes to fd 1 knowing nothing about any redirection.

Every process has a parent, forming a tree rooted at PID 1. Inspect it with `pstree -p` or `ps -ejH`. Three lifecycle states matter in interviews. A **zombie** (state `Z`, shown as `<defunct>`) has exited, but its parent has not yet called `wait()` to collect the exit status. The kernel must retain the exit code and a minimal task entry until someone asks for it, so a zombie holds a PID slot but no memory and no CPU. You cannot kill a zombie — it is already dead. The bug is always in the parent, and the fix is to make the parent reap, or restart it, at which point its zombies are re-parented to PID 1, which reaps them immediately. A handful of zombies is harmless; thousands mean a leaking supervisor and eventual PID exhaustion. An **orphan** is the opposite: the parent died first, so the kernel re-parents the child to PID 1 — or to the nearest ancestor that called `prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER)`, which is how systemd user managers and container runtimes keep track of their trees. A **`D`-state** process is in uninterruptible sleep, almost always inside a kernel I/O path. It cannot be killed, not even with SIGKILL, until that I/O completes or errors out — so a hung NFS mount or a dying disk produces unkillable processes and a load average that climbs with no CPU usage behind it.

Beyond parent and child, processes are grouped twice more: into **process groups** (a pipeline is one group, which is what lets Ctrl-C interrupt every stage of `a | b | c` at once) and into **sessions** with an optional controlling terminal. When the terminal disappears the kernel sends SIGHUP to the foreground group — the reason a long-running command dies when your SSH connection drops, and the reason `nohup`, `setsid`, `tmux`, and `systemd-run --scope` exist.

Your primary window into all of this is `/proc/<pid>`: `cmdline` (NUL-separated argv), `environ` (the environment captured at exec time, a good place to find leaked secrets), `cwd` and `exe` as symlinks, `fd/` with every open descriptor, `status` with UIDs, thread count and memory, `limits` with the effective rlimits, and `stack`/`wchan` describing what a stuck process is blocked on. When a process misbehaves and you cannot attach a debugger, `/proc` plus custom `ps -o` columns will usually tell the story.
sections.code:
# The fork/exec window, spelled out (what your shell does for `ls > out.txt`)
pid = fork()
if pid == 0:                      # child
    fd = open("out.txt", O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666)
    dup2(fd, 1)                   # stdout now points at the file
    close(fd)
    setuid(1000); chdir("/srv/app")
    execve("/usr/bin/ls", ["ls"], environ)   # on success, never returns
else:                             # parent
    waitpid(pid, &status, 0)      # reap the child; skip this and it becomes a zombie

# Find zombies and, more usefully, their parents - the actual bug
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/'
ps -eo stat= | grep -c '^Z'

# Uninterruptible sleep: unkillable, and where mystery load comes from
ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:24,comm | awk '$2 ~ /D/'
cat /proc/1873/stack            # kernel stack: often nfs_*, blk_*, or ext4_* frames

# Everything about a live process, no debugger required
tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/1873/cmdline; echo
ls -l /proc/1873/fd | head            # open files, sockets, pipes
grep -E 'Threads|VmRSS|^Uid' /proc/1873/status
grep -i 'open files' /proc/1873/limits

# Survive a dropped SSH session
setsid --fork long_job.sh >/var/log/long_job.log 2>&1
systemd-run --unit=migrate --collect /usr/local/bin/migrate.sh   # better: supervised + logged

sections.title: 6. Signals and Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
A signal is the kernel's asynchronous notification mechanism: a small integer delivered to a process, interrupting whatever it is doing so it can run a registered handler, or so the kernel can apply a default action (terminate, terminate-and-dump-core, stop, or ignore). On x86-64 the numbers to know are SIGHUP 1, SIGINT 2, SIGQUIT 3, SIGKILL 9, SIGSEGV 11, SIGPIPE 13, SIGTERM 15, SIGCHLD 17, SIGSTOP 19. `kill` sends SIGTERM by default, despite the name.

The distinction interviewers always probe is SIGTERM versus SIGKILL. SIGTERM is a polite request: it is catchable, so a well-written server installs a handler and uses it to stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, flush buffers, deregister from service discovery, and exit cleanly. SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored — the kernel simply tears the process down. No cleanup code runs, so buffered writes are lost and lock files and temp files stay behind, and databases come back needing recovery. That is not a philosophical difference: it is why `kill -9` is a last resort, and why "the deploy keeps leaving stale lock files" usually traces to an orchestrator whose termination grace period is shorter than the app's shutdown path. One case defeats even SIGKILL: a process in `D` state is inside the kernel and will process no signal until the I/O it is waiting on returns.

SIGHUP has an interesting double life. Originally it meant "the modem hung up", and the kernel still sends it to the foreground process group when a terminal disappears — hence `nohup`. Daemons have no terminal, so by convention they repurposed SIGHUP to mean "reload configuration without restarting"; nginx, sshd and rsyslog all do this. SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2 are reserved for the application to define, and nginx uses SIGUSR1 for "reopen log files", which is exactly how logrotate avoids the deleted-but-open-file problem. SIGPIPE matters more than people expect: writing to a pipe or socket whose reader is gone kills you by default. That is *by design* — it is how `zcat huge.gz | head -5` terminates the decompressor instead of decompressing 40 GB — and it is why network servers explicitly ignore SIGPIPE and check `write()` for `EPIPE` instead.

Signals map into exit statuses: a process killed by signal N reports `128 + N` to the shell. `137` is SIGKILL (128+9), and in Kubernetes it almost always means the container hit its memory limit and the cgroup OOM killer fired. `143` is SIGTERM (128+15), the normal result of a clean stop. `130` is Ctrl-C. Recognising those three on sight saves real time in an incident.

PID 1 has special signal semantics, and they bite everyone who containerises an application. For PID 1 the kernel does not apply default actions for signals the process has not explicitly handled — the protection exists so you cannot accidentally kill init. So if your container's main process has no SIGTERM handler, `docker stop` or a pod deletion sends SIGTERM, nothing happens, and after the grace period SIGKILL arrives. Every shutdown becomes a hard kill and every deploy drops connections. There is a second trap: writing `CMD npm start` in shell form makes `/bin/sh -c` your PID 1, and a minimal shell does not forward signals to its children. The fixes are exec form (`CMD ["node", "server.js"]`), `exec`-ing the real binary as the last line of an entrypoint script so it inherits PID 1, or running a tiny init such as `tini` (`docker run --init`) that both forwards signals and reaps orphaned zombies.

Shell scripts have their own quirk worth knowing. Bash does not interrupt a running foreground child to service a trap; the handler fires only after that child returns. A wrapper doing `trap cleanup TERM; long_command` therefore appears to ignore SIGTERM for the entire runtime of `long_command`. To get responsive handling, background the child and `wait` on it, because `wait` is interruptible.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# A wrapper that actually responds to SIGTERM while a long child is running.
set -euo pipefail

child_pid=""
on_term() {
  echo "SIGTERM received, forwarding to child $child_pid" >&2
  [[ -n $child_pid ]] && kill -TERM "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
}
trap on_term TERM INT

/usr/local/bin/server --config /etc/app.yml &
child_pid=$!

# `wait` is interruptible, so the trap runs immediately. When interrupted it returns
# 128+N, so wait a second time to collect the child's real exit status.
wait "$child_pid" || true
wait "$child_pid" 2>/dev/null
rc=$?
echo "child exited rc=$rc"
exit "$rc"

# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Signal cheat-sheet in practice
kill -TERM 1234                     # ask nicely (this is the default)
kill -HUP  "$(cat /run/nginx.pid)"  # reload config, no restart
kill -USR1 "$(cat /run/nginx.pid)"  # reopen log files (post-logrotate)
kill -QUIT 1234                     # terminate + core dump (if ulimit -c allows)
kill -0    1234                     # send nothing: "does this pid exist and may I signal it"
pkill -f 'python worker.py --queue=email'    # match the full command line, not just comm
timeout -s TERM -k 30s 5m ./backup.sh        # TERM at 5m, KILL 30s later if still alive

# Exit codes to recognise instantly
# 130 = 128+2  SIGINT (Ctrl-C)
# 137 = 128+9  SIGKILL  -> in k8s: OOMKilled, or grace period expired
# 143 = 128+15 SIGTERM  -> normal orchestrated stop
# 126 = found but not executable      127 = command not found

# Container shutdown that works
# Dockerfile:
#   ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]
#   CMD ["node", "server.js"]
# entrypoint.sh - the last line MUST exec, or the shell stays PID 1 and eats signals:
#   run_migrations
#   exec "$@"

sections.title: 7. systemd Units: The Dependency Graph and the Service Lifecycle
sections.content:
systemd replaced SysV init because shell-script init had no model of the system. Each `/etc/init.d` script was an opaque program that returned when it felt like it, so ordering was expressed by numeric filename prefixes, "is it running?" meant reading a PID file that might be stale, and there was no reliable way to stop every process a service had spawned. systemd's answer is to make the system a declarative dependency graph of *units*, with the kernel's cgroups as the tracking mechanism.

A unit is a typed object described by an ini-style file: `.service` (a process), `.socket` (a listening socket), `.timer` (a scheduled activation), `.mount` and `.automount`, `.target` (a synchronisation point, the rough equivalent of a runlevel), `.path`, `.slice` and `.scope`. Files are searched in a fixed precedence order — `/etc/systemd/system` (administrator, wins) overrides `/run/systemd/system` (runtime) overrides `/usr/lib/systemd/system` (packages). You should never edit a vendor file in `/usr/lib`; use `systemctl edit foo.service`, which creates a drop-in at `/etc/systemd/system/foo.service.d/override.conf` containing only your changes so package updates keep working. One trap with drop-ins: directives that accumulate as lists, such as `ExecStart=` and `Environment=`, are *appended* rather than replaced, so to change one you must first assign it the empty value to clear the list, then set the new one. Always run `systemctl daemon-reload` after editing units, and `systemctl cat foo` to see the final merged result.

The two dependency axes are independent, and confusing them is the classic interview trip-wire. `Requires=`, `Wants=` and `BindsTo=` express *requirement*: whether the other unit gets pulled in, and what happens if it fails or stops. `After=` and `Before=` express only *ordering*. `Requires=b.service` with no `After=b.service` means systemd starts both at the same time and your service may well come up before its dependency is ready — the graph says "b must be running" but nothing said "wait for it". `Wants=` is the soft version: pull it in, but do not fail if it does not start, and it is what you almost always want between loosely coupled services. `BindsTo=` is the strict version: if the bound unit stops for any reason, this one stops too — appropriate for a service tied to a device or a mount.

`Type=` tells systemd how to decide a service has finished starting. `simple` (the default) considers the service started as soon as the process is forked, which means anything ordered after it may race with its real readiness. `exec` is slightly stronger: it waits until `execve` succeeds. `forking` is for classic daemons that background themselves, and needs `PIDFile=` so systemd can follow the right child. `oneshot` is for a command that runs and exits, usually with `RemainAfterExit=yes` so the unit counts as active afterwards. `notify` is the honest one: the service calls `sd_notify(READY=1)` when it is genuinely ready to serve, so ordering means something. If a question asks how to guarantee a dependent service starts only after another can actually accept traffic, the answers are `Type=notify`, socket activation, or an explicit `ExecStartPre` health check — not `Type=simple` plus hope.

Restart behaviour is where production bites. `Restart=on-failure` (or `always`) plus `RestartSec=` gives you supervision, but systemd also applies a rate limit: by default `StartLimitBurst=5` starts inside `StartLimitIntervalSec=10s` puts the unit into a permanent `failed` state with "start request repeated too quickly", and no further restarts happen until you run `systemctl reset-failed`. Every engineer meets this at least once while debugging a crash-looping service and wondering why the restarts stopped. On shutdown, systemd sends `SIGTERM` to every process in the unit's cgroup (`KillMode=control-group` is the default, which is why stray children get cleaned up too), waits `TimeoutStopSec=` — 90 seconds by default — and then sends `SIGKILL`.

Because every unit gets its own cgroup, you get accounting and limits for free: `MemoryMax=`, `MemoryHigh=`, `CPUQuota=`, `TasksMax=`, `IOWeight=`. And systemd doubles as a sandbox: `NoNewPrivileges=`, `PrivateTmp=`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `ProtectHome=`, `ReadWritePaths=`, `DynamicUser=`, `CapabilityBoundingSet=` and `SystemCallFilter=@system-service` let you confine a plain binary without a container. `systemd-analyze security foo.service` will grade your unit and tell you what is still exposed.
sections.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/checkout-api.service
[Unit]
Description=Checkout API
Documentation=https://wiki.internal/checkout
# ordering AND requirement - you need both
After=network-online.target postgresql.service
Wants=network-online.target
Requires=postgresql.service
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=notify                 # the app calls sd_notify(READY=1) when it can serve
NotifyAccess=main
User=checkout
Group=checkout
WorkingDirectory=/srv/checkout
EnvironmentFile=/etc/checkout/env        # KEY=VALUE lines, chmod 640
ExecStartPre=/usr/local/bin/checkout migrate --check
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/checkout serve --config /etc/checkout/config.yml
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
TimeoutStopSec=30s          # must exceed the app's graceful drain time

# resource limits, no container required
MemoryMax=2G
CPUQuota=150%               # 1.5 cores
TasksMax=512
LimitNOFILE=65535

# sandboxing
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/checkout /var/log/checkout
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
UMask=0027

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now checkout-api        # enable = create the WantedBy symlink
systemctl cat checkout-api                 # merged view: vendor file + all drop-ins
systemctl show -p Restart -p TimeoutStopSec checkout-api    # effective values
systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/checkout-api.service
systemd-analyze security checkout-api
systemctl list-dependencies checkout-api --all
systemctl reset-failed checkout-api        # clear the start-rate-limit lockout
systemd-analyze blame | head -10           # slowest units at boot

sections.title: 8. Scheduling Work: cron, systemd Timers, and Why Your Job Only Fails at 3am
sections.content:
cron is a daemon that wakes every minute, compares the current time against every crontab entry, and forks a shell for anything that matches. The format is five time fields — minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week — followed by the command. User crontabs are edited with `crontab -e` and have no user field; system files in `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d` insert a user field in the sixth position. Two quirks of the schedule syntax are worth memorising because they produce real incidents. Day-of-week accepts both 0 and 7 for Sunday. And if *both* day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted (neither is `*`), cron runs the job when **either** matches, not both — so `0 0 13 * 5` fires on every Friday *and* on the 13th, which is rarely what the author meant.

The reason "it works when I run it by hand but not from cron" is the most common cron question is that cron gives your job an almost empty environment. It does not source `/etc/profile`, `~/.bashrc` or `~/.profile`. `PATH` is a minimal default (typically `/usr/bin:/bin`), `SHELL` is `/bin/sh` rather than bash, `HOME` is set from the passwd entry, and everything else your interactive session accumulated — `JAVA_HOME`, virtualenv activation, `AWS_PROFILE`, locale, `TERM` — is simply absent. There is no TTY, so anything that prompts or expects a terminal breaks. The disciplined fix is to make the job self-contained: absolute paths for every binary, explicit `PATH=` and any needed variables at the top of the crontab or sourced from a file inside the script, and never rely on the current working directory. One more genuine gotcha: in a crontab, `%` is special — an unescaped `%` becomes a newline and everything after the first one is fed to the command's stdin — so `date +%F` must be written `date +\%F`.

Output handling is the other half. cron mails anything a job writes to stdout or stderr to the `MAILTO` address, and on a box with no MTA that mail vanishes, which is how jobs fail silently for months. Redirect explicitly to a log file, and do not blanket-redirect to `/dev/null` — that discards the error messages you will one day need. Add `flock` if overlapping runs would corrupt anything: a five-minute job that occasionally takes six minutes will otherwise pile up until the machine falls over.

systemd timers do the same job with more machinery and better observability. A timer is two units: `backup.timer` with a `[Timer]` section, and `backup.service` (`Type=oneshot`) with the actual command. The advantages are concrete. `OnCalendar=` takes a richer, validated syntax you can test with `systemd-analyze calendar "Mon *-*-* 04:00:00"`. `Persistent=true` runs a missed job at next boot, so a laptop or an instance that was down at 3am still gets its backup — cron simply skips it. `RandomizedDelaySec=` spreads a fleet's jobs out so 500 machines do not hit the artifact server in the same second. Timers can also be relative: `OnBootSec=`, `OnUnitActiveSec=` for "every 15 minutes after the last run finished", which naturally prevents overlap. The job runs as a normal unit, so it gets journal logs, `systemctl status backup.service`, resource limits, sandboxing, and a real exit status; `systemctl list-timers` shows the next and last firing for everything. One default that surprises people: timers have `AccuracySec=1min`, meaning systemd may fire up to a minute late in order to batch wakeups and save power. If you need precision, set `AccuracySec=1s`.

Which to choose? Timers, on any systemd host, for anything that matters — the observability alone is worth it. cron remains fine for simple, tolerant jobs and is still the only option in minimal containers and on non-systemd systems. Either way, the job itself should be idempotent, should log to a known place, should be locked against overlap, and should emit a heartbeat to your monitoring, because the failure mode you actually need to catch is not a failing job but a job that stopped running at all.
sections.code:
# ---------- crontab, written defensively ----------
SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
MAILTO=sre-alerts@example.com

# m  h dom mon dow  command
  */5 *  *   *   *  /usr/bin/flock -n /run/lock/sync.lock /usr/local/bin/sync.sh >> /var/log/sync.log 2>&1
  17  3  *   *   *  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh --date="$(date +\%F)" >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
# careful: below fires on EVERY Friday and on the 13th (dom and dow are OR'ed)
  0   0  13  *   5  /usr/local/bin/spooky.sh

# ---------- the systemd equivalent ----------
# /etc/systemd/system/backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly backup
[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=backup
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh
# systemd runs only one instance of a given unit at a time -> no flock needed

# /etc/systemd/system/backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run nightly backup at 03:17
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:17:00
Persistent=true             # catch up after downtime (cron would just skip)
RandomizedDelaySec=600      # spread the fleet over 10 minutes
AccuracySec=1s              # default is 1min
Unit=backup.service         # implied by the name; shown for clarity
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

systemctl enable --now backup.timer
systemctl list-timers --all
systemd-analyze calendar "Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00:00"    # validate before you ship it
journalctl -u backup.service --since "2 days ago"

# ---------- locking inside the script itself (works under cron or anywhere) ----------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
exec 9>/run/lock/backup.lock
flock -n 9 || { echo "previous run still going; exiting" >&2; exit 0; }
# ... work ...  (the lock is released when the process exits and fd 9 closes)

sections.title: 9. Package Managers: dpkg/apt, rpm/dnf, and Making Installs Repeatable
sections.content:
Every distribution's package system has two layers, and knowing which layer you are talking to explains most of the confusing behaviour. The **low layer** — `dpkg` on Debian/Ubuntu, `rpm` on RHEL/Fedora/SUSE — installs, removes and queries a single package file that is already sitting on disk. It verifies the archive, unpacks files, runs maintainer scripts, and records everything in a local database. What it will not do is find dependencies: `dpkg -i foo.deb` fails with "dependency problems" and leaves the package half-configured. The **high layer** — `apt` / `apt-get`, `dnf` (successor to `yum`), `zypper` — knows about remote repositories, resolves the dependency graph, downloads what is needed in the right order, and hands the files to the low layer.

A repository is an HTTP directory of packages plus signed index metadata. Trust flows from the signature: the index is signed with the repo's GPG key, the index contains cryptographic hashes of every package, and the client verifies the signature and then the hashes. That chain is why adding a third-party repository is a real trust decision — the key you install can authorise arbitrary root-level code on your machines. On modern Debian and Ubuntu the old global `apt-key` keyring is deprecated and removed; the correct pattern is to drop the key in `/usr/share/keyrings/vendor.gpg` and scope it to exactly one source with `signed-by=` in the sources entry, so that key can only vouch for that one repo.

The commands that matter day to day: `apt-get update` refreshes the indexes and never installs anything (forgetting it is why you get 404s on package fetch after a mirror rotates); `apt-get install` installs; `apt-get upgrade` upgrades packages without removing anything, while `full-upgrade`/`dist-upgrade` is allowed to remove packages to satisfy a new dependency graph. For queries, `dpkg -l` lists installed packages with a two-letter state (`ii` = installed, `rc` = removed but config files remain), `dpkg -L pkg` lists the files a package owns, and `dpkg -S /path/to/file` answers the very useful reverse question "which package put this here?". The dnf equivalents are `rpm -qa`, `rpm -ql`, `rpm -qf`, plus `rpm -V` which verifies installed files against the recorded hashes and modes — an excellent quick integrity check. `dnf history` and `dnf history undo <id>` give you a transaction log and rollback, which apt does not offer natively.

Three production concerns separate a strong answer from a shallow one. First, **non-interactivity**: automation must set `DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` and decide in advance what happens to modified config files, because dpkg will otherwise stop and prompt when a package ships a new version of a conffile you edited (`-o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold` keeps yours, `--force-confnew` takes theirs). A pipeline that hangs at 2am on a purple ncurses dialog is a rite of passage. Second, **version control**: `apt-get install nginx` installs whatever is current today, which means two machines built a week apart are not the same machine. Pin exact versions (`apt-get install nginx=1.24.0-2ubuntu7`), use `apt-mark hold` or dnf's `versionlock` to stop a package moving, and prefer building an image once and deploying that image everywhere over running `apt-get upgrade` on live hosts. Third, **restart awareness**: upgrading a shared library does not restart the processes that already mapped the old one. Until you restart them they keep running the vulnerable code, and `lsof` will show them holding `(deleted)` library files. `needrestart` on Debian/Ubuntu and `dnf needs-restarting -r` on RHEL tell you which services — or whether the kernel — still need a restart. This is precisely why patching is not finished when the package manager exits.

Finally, `/usr/local` and `/opt` exist so that things you install by hand do not collide with the package manager. Mixing `make install` into `/usr` and then wondering why an upgrade overwrote your binary is a self-inflicted wound; and where a language-level installer is unavoidable (pip, npm, gem), keep it inside a virtualenv or a container rather than letting it write into system directories.
sections.code:
# ---------- Debian / Ubuntu ----------
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends nginx=1.24.0-2ubuntu7
apt-mark hold nginx                     # stop it moving on the next upgrade
apt-cache policy nginx                  # installed vs candidate vs available versions
apt-get -y -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold upgrade    # keep MY config files

dpkg -l | grep '^rc'                    # removed but config left behind (purge with apt purge)
dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx                 # which package owns this file?
dpkg -L nginx | head                    # which files does this package own?
apt-get autoremove --purge ; apt-get clean

# Third-party repo, the modern (apt-key-free) way
curl -fsSL https://example.com/gpg | gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/vendor.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/vendor.gpg] https://example.com/apt stable main" \
  > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/vendor.list

# ---------- RHEL / Fedora ----------
dnf install -y nginx-1.24.0
dnf versionlock add nginx
rpm -qa | grep openssl
rpm -qf /usr/sbin/nginx                 # owning package
rpm -V nginx                            # verify files against the package database
dnf history                             # transaction log
dnf history undo 42                     # roll a transaction back
dnf needs-restarting -r                 # does the KERNEL need a reboot? (rc 1 = yes)

# ---------- after any library/security upgrade ----------
needrestart -r l                        # Debian/Ubuntu: list services on stale libraries
lsof -nP | grep 'DEL\|(deleted)' | grep -E '\.so' | awk '{print $1, $2}' | sort -u

sections.title: 10. Disk, Inodes, and Why df Disagrees With du
sections.content:
`df` and `du` answer different questions using different data, and an interviewer asking "df says full, du says half empty — explain" is testing whether you know that. `df` asks the *filesystem* for its accounting: it reads superblock counters of total, used and free blocks. It is O(1), it includes every allocated block whether or not anything can reach it, and it is authoritative about how full the device is. `du` walks a directory tree, stats every file it can reach, and sums the blocks those files occupy. It is O(number of files), it can only count what is reachable through the tree it is given, and by default it reports *allocated* blocks rather than apparent size.

That difference produces four distinct real-world causes for a gap, and a good answer walks through them in order of likelihood. **One: a deleted file that is still open.** Someone ran `rm` on a huge log while the process had it open; the directory entry is gone so `du` cannot see it, but the blocks stay allocated until the last descriptor closes. Find it with `lsof -nP +L1`, and fix it by restarting or signalling the process, or by truncating through `/proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`. **Two: files hidden under a mount point.** Data was written to a directory before the intended disk was mounted there; the mount now shadows it, so `du` cannot reach those files while the blocks are still consumed. Bind-mount the root elsewhere to look underneath. **Three: reserved blocks.** ext4 reserves 5% of the filesystem for root by default so that a full disk does not stop root from logging in and fixing it; `df`'s Avail column excludes that reserve, which is why Use% can read 100% while a few gigabytes remain. On a large pure-data volume, `tune2fs -m 1` recovers most of it. **Four: sparse files and hard links.** `du` counts allocated blocks, so a sparse file (a VM image, a preallocated database file) shows far less than its apparent size, and `du --apparent-size` shows more; and `du` counts a set of hard links to the same inode only once, so a backup tree full of hard links looks much smaller than the sum of its parts.

Then there is the failure that looks identical from the application's point of view but is not about space at all: **inode exhaustion**. Every file needs an inode, ext4 fixes the inode count at `mkfs` time, and a directory tree full of millions of tiny files — PHP sessions, mail spool, unrotated per-request log files, an unpruned cache — can exhaust them while blocks remain plentiful. `write()` returns `ENOSPC`, "No space left on device", and `df -h` shows 55% used. The tell is `df -i` at 100%. You cannot grow ext4's inode table in place; the fix is to delete files (carefully — `rm` on millions of files is itself slow and I/O heavy, `find ... -delete` is better than `rm $(find ...)`), or to reformat with `-N`/`-i` tuning, or to move to XFS which allocates inodes dynamically.

Triage discipline for "disk full" is worth rehearsing until it is muscle memory, because it happens under pressure. Confirm which filesystem: `df -hT`. Check inodes: `df -i`. Descend by size, always with `-x` so you stay on one filesystem and do not wander into `/proc` or a network mount: `du -xhd1 /` then repeat down the biggest child, or use `ncdu -x /`. If nothing accounts for it, check unlinked-but-open files and then look under mount points. Only then start deleting — and prefer truncating an active log to deleting it, because deleting is the move that creates the invisible-space problem in the first place. Keep a couple of structural defences in place too: put `/var/log` and container storage on their own filesystems so a runaway log cannot take the root filesystem — and therefore the whole machine — down with it, make sure logrotate actually covers your application's logs, and alert on disk usage at a threshold that leaves you time to act rather than at 99%.
sections.code:
# ---------- the disk-full runbook ----------
df -hT                       # which filesystem, and what type
df -i                        # inodes: a separate way to be "full"
du -xhd1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -15      # -x: do not cross filesystem boundaries
du -xhd1 /var | sort -h | tail
ncdu -x /var                 # interactive, if installed

# Biggest individual files on this filesystem
find / -xdev -type f -size +500M -printf '%s\t%p\n' 2>/dev/null | sort -rn | head

# Unlinked but still open (space held by a running process)
lsof -nP +L1
# Space hidden underneath a mount point
mount --bind / /mnt/underlay && du -xhd2 /mnt/underlay | sort -h | tail && umount /mnt/underlay

# Reclaim without breaking a running writer
truncate -s 0 /var/log/app/huge.log            # keeps the inode + open fds valid
journalctl --disk-usage
journalctl --vacuum-size=500M                  # or --vacuum-time=7d
apt-get clean                                  # /var/cache/apt/archives
docker system df && docker system prune -af --volumes    # usually the real answer on a node

# ext4 reserved blocks: 5% by default, invisible to non-root
tune2fs -l /dev/nvme0n1p2 | grep -i 'reserved block count'
tune2fs -m 1 /dev/nvme0n1p2                    # 5% -> 1% on a big data volume

# Grow a filesystem online (LVM + ext4/xfs)
lvextend -L +20G /dev/mapper/vg0-data
resize2fs /dev/mapper/vg0-data                 # ext4
xfs_growfs /data                               # xfs (grow only; xfs cannot shrink)

# Deleting millions of files without melting the box
find /var/cache/app -xdev -type f -mtime +7 -delete      # no exec, no giant argv

sections.title: 11. Logs, Rotation, and journalctl
sections.content:
Linux logging has two overlapping systems, and you need both. The traditional one is syslog: applications hand a message plus a facility (auth, cron, daemon, mail, local0-7) and a severity (emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug) to a daemon such as rsyslog, which routes it to plain text files under `/var/log` and optionally forwards it over the network. The modern one is systemd's journald, which receives messages from the kernel ring buffer, from unit stdout/stderr, and from the syslog socket, and stores them in an indexed binary format with structured metadata attached to every entry — the unit, PID, UID, executable path, boot ID, and any custom fields the application supplied. Most distributions run both, with journald forwarding to rsyslog for the text files that existing tooling expects.

The binary format is a real trade-off. You cannot `grep` the journal directly, and a corrupted journal file is harder to salvage than a truncated text log. What you get in exchange is indexed, typed querying that text files cannot match: filter by unit, by boot, by time range, by priority, by arbitrary field, all without regex gymnastics. `journalctl -u nginx -S "1 hour ago" -p err` is precise in a way that `grep` over rotated, compressed text files is not. Learn the flags that matter: `-u UNIT`, `-f` to follow, `-n N` for the last N lines, `-b` for the current boot and `-b -1` for the previous one (the fastest way to investigate an unexplained reboot), `-k` for kernel messages, `-p err` for priority and above, `--since`/`--until`, `-o json` for machine consumption, `-o cat` for bare messages, and `_PID=`/`_UID=`/`_COMM=` for field matching.

A detail that catches people out: by default on many systems the journal is *volatile*, stored in `/run/log/journal`, which is tmpfs and therefore gone after a reboot. If the logs from before a crash matter — and they always do — the journal must be persistent, which means `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` and the `/var/log/journal` directory existing. Size is bounded by `SystemMaxUse=`, which defaults to 10% of the filesystem capped at 4 GiB; check current usage with `journalctl --disk-usage` and reclaim with `journalctl --vacuum-size=` or `--vacuum-time=`. journald also rate-limits: past `RateLimitBurst` messages within `RateLimitIntervalSec` from one service it drops the rest and logs "Suppressed N messages". A chatty service under load therefore loses exactly the log lines you need during the incident, which is an argument both for tuning those values on known-noisy units and for not logging at debug level in production.

For text logs, `logrotate` handles rotation, and the way it interacts with open file descriptors is a genuinely good interview question. The default mode renames `app.log` to `app.log.1` and creates a fresh `app.log`. But a running process holds a descriptor to the *inode*, not the name, so it happily continues writing into the renamed — and later compressed or deleted — file. New log lines vanish, and if the old file was deleted the disk space is never released. There are two correct fixes. The clean one is `postrotate`: signal the application to reopen its log files (nginx uses SIGUSR1, many daemons use SIGHUP), so it picks up the new inode. The blunt one is `copytruncate`: copy the contents aside and then truncate the original in place, which keeps the inode and therefore the descriptor valid, at the cost of losing any lines written between the copy and the truncate, and of briefly doubling the disk usage. Use `postrotate` when the app supports reopening, `copytruncate` only when it does not.

Two design points to raise unprompted. Applications running under systemd or in containers should log to stdout and stderr and let the platform handle collection, rather than managing their own files and rotation. And local logs are for debugging one machine; anything you need for correlation, alerting or audit has to be shipped off the host — because the failure you most need to investigate is the one where the host is gone.
sections.code:
# ---------- journalctl, the flags you will actually use ----------
journalctl -u checkout-api -f                  # follow one unit
journalctl -u checkout-api -n 200 --no-pager
journalctl -b                                  # this boot
journalctl -b -1 -p err                        # errors from the PREVIOUS boot (crash forensics)
journalctl -k --since "30 min ago"             # kernel ring buffer, e.g. OOM kills
journalctl --since "2026-03-01 09:00" --until "2026-03-01 09:15"
journalctl _COMM=sshd -p warning
journalctl -u checkout-api -o json | jq -r 'select(.PRIORITY<="3") | .MESSAGE'
journalctl -g 'timeout|refused' -u checkout-api     # regex search (systemd 237+)
journalctl --disk-usage ; journalctl --vacuum-time=14d
journalctl --list-boots                        # map boot IDs to timestamps

# Make the journal survive reboots (/etc/systemd/journald.conf)
[Journal]
Storage=persistent
SystemMaxUse=2G
SystemMaxFileSize=200M
RateLimitIntervalSec=30s
RateLimitBurst=10000        # raise for a legitimately chatty service
# then: mkdir -p /var/log/journal && systemctl restart systemd-journald

# ---------- logrotate: the two correct strategies ----------
# /etc/logrotate.d/checkout   (preferred: tell the app to reopen)
/var/log/checkout/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress          # do not compress the most recent rotation yet
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 checkout adm
    sharedscripts
    postrotate
        /bin/systemctl kill -s HUP checkout-api.service 2>/dev/null || true
    endscript
}

# Only when the app cannot reopen its own logs:
/var/log/legacy/*.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    copytruncate           # keeps the inode alive; loses lines written mid-copy
}

logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/checkout      # dry run - ALWAYS do this first
logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/checkout      # force a rotation now
systemctl list-timers logrotate.timer

sections.title: 12. Users, Groups, Identity, and sudo
sections.content:
To the kernel a user is just a number. Every process carries a real UID, an effective UID (the one used for permission checks), a saved UID, and a filesystem UID, plus the same set for groups and a list of supplementary group IDs. Names exist purely for humans, and the mapping lives in userspace. That has a practical consequence people meet when they copy files into a container or onto a NAS: the file records UID 1000, and whether that is `alice` or `deploy` depends entirely on which host's name database you ask.

`/etc/passwd` is world-readable and holds seven colon-separated fields: name, a legacy password field that is now always `x`, UID, primary GID, a comment/GECOS field, home directory, and login shell. The hashes moved out decades ago into `/etc/shadow`, which is mode 0640 root:shadow, and holds the hash plus password ageing policy. A modern hash looks like `$6$...` (SHA-512-crypt) or `$y$...` (yescrypt, now the default on recent Debian/Ubuntu); a `!` or `*` where the hash should be means no password login is possible. `/etc/group` maps group names to GIDs and lists supplementary members. The convention on most distributions is that UIDs below 1000 are system accounts and human users start at 1000, configured by `UID_MIN` in `/etc/login.defs`.

Read identity through NSS, not by grepping files. The Name Service Switch, configured in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`, lets identity come from local files, LDAP, SSSD, or a directory service — so `grep alice /etc/passwd` returns nothing on a domain-joined host while `getent passwd alice` returns the right answer. `id alice` shows UID, primary GID and all supplementary groups, and is the first command to run when a permission problem does not make sense.

The single most common group question in interviews: you add a user to a group and it does not take effect. Group membership is resolved at login and baked into the process credentials, which are then inherited by every child. An existing shell — and every process it spawned, including your SSH session and any running service — keeps the old group list until it is replaced. The user must log out and back in, or start a new session; `newgrp docker` opens a subshell with the new group as a workaround, and for a daemon you restart the service. `id` in the old shell will keep showing the old list, which is what makes it confusing.

Service accounts deserve their own rules. Create them with `useradd --system --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --home-dir /nonexistent`, so nothing can log in as them interactively, and give each service its own account so a compromise of one does not grant access to another's data. Even better on systemd, `DynamicUser=yes` allocates a transient UID for the lifetime of the service, so there is no persistent account to attack at all. Never run application code as root because "it's easier": the whole point of the UID model is that a bug in your code should not be a bug in your kernel's threat model.

`sudo` provides controlled escalation with an audit trail. Every invocation is logged with the user, the terminal, the working directory, the target user and the exact command, which is the property that makes it better than sharing the root password. Rules live in `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/sudoers.d/*`, and you edit them with `visudo`, which syntax-checks before installing — a broken sudoers file can lock every administrator out of a machine at once. The standard grant is membership in `wheel` (RHEL) or `sudo` (Debian). `sudo -l` shows what the current user is permitted. Credentials are cached per terminal for a short period (five minutes by default) so you are not prompted on every command.

The hard part is writing least-privilege rules that actually restrict anything. Granting a specific command sounds safe but frequently is not, because many programs can spawn a shell: `sudo vi`, `sudo less`, `sudo find ... -exec`, `sudo awk 'BEGIN{system("/bin/sh")}'`, and anything with a `!command` escape hands over a root shell immediately. Wildcards are worse — `NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart *` lets the user restart any unit including ones they should not touch, and a rule ending in a wildcard path can often be walked with `..`. Prefer `sudoedit` over `sudo vi` for file editing, point rules at small purpose-built wrapper scripts you control rather than at general-purpose tools, avoid `NOPASSWD` except for genuinely non-interactive automation, and remember that a user who can run *any* command as root is root — the rule is documentation, not a boundary.
