# Identity: always through NSS, so LDAP/SSSD-backed users resolve too
id deploy
getent passwd deploy            # works with files, LDAP, SSSD, ...
getent group docker
groups deploy

# /etc/passwd fields
# name:x:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell
deploy:x:1001:1001:Deploy Robot:/home/deploy:/bin/bash
nginx:x:113:119::/nonexistent:/usr/sbin/nologin

# A proper service account
useradd --system --shell /usr/sbin/nologin --home-dir /nonexistent \
        --comment "checkout api" checkout
usermod -aG appdata checkout     # -a is critical: without it you REPLACE the group list
# ...then restart the service; a running process keeps its old credentials.

# Why "I added myself to docker but it still says permission denied"
$ sudo usermod -aG docker alice
$ id                       # old shell: docker is NOT listed
$ newgrp docker            # subshell with the new group, or just log out and back in

# Password / account state
chage -l alice             # ageing policy and expiry
passwd -l svcuser          # lock the password (still allows key-based SSH!)
usermod --expiredate 1 svcuser   # actually disable the account

# ---------- sudoers (always edit with visudo) ----------
# /etc/sudoers.d/oncall   -> visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/oncall
%oncall ALL=(root) /usr/local/bin/restart-checkout, /usr/bin/journalctl -u checkout-api *
Defaults:%oncall  timestamp_timeout=5, log_output
Defaults  logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"

# DANGEROUS grants that are really "full root":
#   %devs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vi        -> :!sh
#   %devs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find      -> find . -exec /bin/sh \;
#   %devs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/awk       -> awk 'BEGIN{system("/bin/sh")}'
#   %devs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/chmod         -> chmod u+s /bin/bash

sudo -l                     # what am I allowed to run?
sudo -u checkout -i         # become the service account for debugging
journalctl -t sudo --since today       # the audit trail

sections.title: 13. SSH and Key-Based Authentication
sections.content:
SSH does three things in one protocol: it authenticates the *server* to you, authenticates *you* to the server, and encrypts everything in between. Getting the order right is the whole answer to "how does SSH key auth work", because candidates routinely describe only the second half.

The connection opens with a plaintext version exchange, then a key exchange — typically ECDH over Curve25519 — that produces a shared session key neither side transmitted. Within that exchange the server signs a transcript with its **host key** private key and sends the corresponding public key. Your client compares that public key against `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. On the first connection there is nothing to compare, so it prints the fingerprint and asks you to confirm: this is trust on first use, and it is the protocol's real weak point, because clicking "yes" without verifying the fingerprint out of band means a man-in-the-middle on that first connection wins permanently. Once recorded, a mismatch produces the loud `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED` banner, which usually means an instance was rebuilt and reused an IP, but occasionally means exactly what it says. At scale, SSH certificates solve this properly: you trust one CA in `known_hosts` via `@cert-authority`, and every host presents a certificate signed by it, so rebuilt hosts never trigger warnings and you never distribute host keys.

Only after that encrypted, server-authenticated channel exists does *user* authentication start. With `publickey`, the client offers a public key; if the server finds a matching line in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` for the target account, it challenges the client, and the client signs data that includes the unique session identifier with the private key. The server verifies with the public key it already had. Two properties fall out of this and are worth stating explicitly in an interview: the private key never leaves your machine and is never sent over the wire, and because the signature is bound to that session's identifier, a captured signature cannot be replayed against a different connection. The `authorized_keys` file is the authoritative list of who can log into an account, which makes it a high-value target — anyone who can write to it grants themselves permanent access, and it is one of the first files to check during an incident.

The most common practical failure is permissions. sshd's `StrictModes` refuses to use `authorized_keys` if the file, `~/.ssh`, or the home directory is writable by group or other, because that would let someone else add a key. The rule is home `755` or tighter, `~/.ssh` `700`, `authorized_keys` `600`, all owned by the user. The failure is silent from the client's point of view — you just get asked for a password — so the diagnosis is always `ssh -vvv` on the client plus the server's own log via `journalctl -u ssh`. On SELinux systems there is an extra trap: a `~/.ssh` created by copying files in can have the wrong security context, and `restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh` fixes it.

Key hygiene: prefer `ed25519` (small, fast, no parameter choices to get wrong) or RSA at 3072 bits or more. Note that OpenSSH 8.8 disabled the `ssh-rsa` *signature algorithm* — SHA-1 — by default; RSA keys still work fine using the `rsa-sha2-256`/`rsa-sha2-512` signature algorithms, so the fix for a legacy server rejecting your RSA key is usually upgrading the server, not regenerating the key. Passphrase-protect private keys and use `ssh-agent` so you type it once.

Server hardening is a standard follow-up: `PasswordAuthentication no` and `PubkeyAuthentication yes` remove password brute-force entirely; `PermitRootLogin no` (or `prohibit-password` where automation needs it) forces named accounts and preserves the audit trail; restrict access with `AllowUsers`/`AllowGroups`; keep a second session open while you reload sshd so a bad config does not lock you out; and validate first with `sshd -t`, inspecting the effective merged configuration with `sshd -T`. Remember that `sshd_config` is first-match-wins for most keywords, so an `Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` at the top of the file means drop-ins win — put your settings there rather than fighting the main file.

Finally, two client features that come up constantly. Agent forwarding (`-A`) exposes your agent socket on the remote host, and anyone with root there can use your agent to authenticate as you to anything you can reach — so prefer `ProxyJump` (`-J bastion`), which tunnels the connection through the bastion while the authentication happens locally, end to end. And `ControlMaster`/`ControlPersist` multiplexing reuses one TCP connection for subsequent sessions to the same host, which turns a 300 ms handshake into an instant login and dramatically speeds up tools such as Ansible.
sections.code:
# ---------- client: ~/.ssh/config is the highest-leverage file you own ----------
Host bastion
    HostName bastion.prod.example.com
    User deploy
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_prod
    IdentitiesOnly yes            # stop offering every key in the agent

Host 10.0.*.*
    ProxyJump bastion             # auth stays LOCAL; far safer than -A
    User deploy
    StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new
    ServerAliveInterval 30
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p
    ControlPersist 10m            # reuse the TCP connection for 10 minutes

# ---------- key setup ----------
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop-2026"
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub deploy@host      # appends, sets modes correctly
ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                  # fingerprint, to verify out of band

# Permissions - the #1 cause of "it keeps asking for a password"
chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 700 ~
restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh          # RHEL/SELinux: wrong context breaks key auth silently

# Debugging, both ends
ssh -vvv deploy@host 2>&1 | grep -Ei 'offering|authentications|denied|publickey'
journalctl -u ssh -n 50        # server side: "Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes"

# Restrict what a key may do (authorized_keys options, evaluated by sshd)
restrict,command="/usr/local/bin/backup-receiver",from="10.0.5.0/24" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3... backup@ci

# ---------- server hardening: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf ----------
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AllowGroups ssh-users
X11Forwarding no
MaxAuthTries 3
ClientAliveInterval 300
LoginGraceTime 20

sshd -t                        # syntax check BEFORE reloading
sshd -T | grep -Ei 'permitrootlogin|passwordauth|allowgroups'   # effective config
systemctl reload ssh           # keep an existing session open while you do this

sections.title: 14. Finding Things: grep, find, and xargs
sections.content:
`grep` prints lines matching a pattern, and the flags that earn their keep are `-r` (recursive), `-n` (line numbers), `-i` (case-insensitive), `-v` (invert), `-c` (count of matching *lines*, not matches), `-l` (just filenames), `-o` (print only the matched part, which is how you extract fields with a regex), `-w` (whole word), `-A`/`-B`/`-C` for context lines, and `--include`/`--exclude-dir` to control what a recursive search touches. Three notes that separate confident use from cargo-culting. Default `grep` uses POSIX basic regular expressions where `+`, `?`, `|`, `(` and `)` must be backslash-escaped; `-E` gives extended syntax where they do not; `-P` gives PCRE with lookarounds, lazy quantifiers and `\d`, but is not available in every build. `-F` treats the pattern as a fixed string, which is both faster and the correct choice whenever the pattern comes from a variable, since otherwise a stray `.` or `*` in user data silently changes the match. And always quote the pattern, or the shell will glob it before grep ever sees it.

`find` is a small declarative language, not a flag soup, and reading it that way makes it click. It walks a tree and evaluates an expression against every entry; tests such as `-name`, `-type`, `-mtime`, `-size`, `-user`, `-perm` return true or false, and they are joined by implicit AND, with `-o` for OR, `!` for NOT, and parentheses (escaped from the shell) for grouping. Actions such as `-print`, `-delete`, `-exec` and `-printf` are also expression terms, evaluated left to right, which is why order matters: `find . -name '*.log' -delete` and `find . -delete -name '*.log'` do very different things, the second one deleting everything before it ever checks the name. `-maxdepth`/`-mindepth` and `-prune` must appear before the tests they are meant to constrain. Time tests are in 24-hour units with truncation, so `-mtime +7` means "modified at least 8 days ago" and `-mtime 0` means "within the last 24 hours"; use `-mmin` when you need minutes. Two options belong in nearly every production `find`: `-xdev` to avoid wandering across mount points into `/proc`, `/sys` or a network filesystem, and quoting around glob patterns so the shell does not expand them first.

`xargs` reads items from stdin and builds command lines from them, which is how you bridge "a list of things" to "a command that takes arguments". Its default behaviour, however, is genuinely dangerous: it splits on whitespace *and* interprets quotes and backslashes, so a filename containing a space becomes two arguments and a filename containing a newline becomes two files. `find . | xargs rm` on a directory containing `my report.pdf` deletes `my` and `report.pdf` if they happen to exist. The fix is a NUL-separated stream, which is the one byte that cannot appear in a filename: `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 ...`. GNU `xargs -r` avoids running the command at all when input is empty, another common source of surprise. `-n` limits items per invocation, `-P` runs invocations in parallel, and `-I{}` substitutes each item into a template (implying one item per run, so it is slower).

Between `-exec cmd {} \;` and `-exec cmd {} +` there is a real difference: the first forks once per file, the second batches as many files as fit onto a command line, exactly like `xargs`. For 100,000 files that is the difference between minutes and seconds. Prefer `+` unless the command genuinely takes one file at a time. And when you need to run something more complex, `find -print0 | xargs -0 -P8 -n50 sh -c '...' _` gives you parallel batches safely.

Two closing practicalities. `grep -r` is fine, but on a large source tree `ripgrep` (`rg`) is dramatically faster because it respects ignore files and searches in parallel; know it exists, and know that it is not installed on the production box you are SSHed into at 3am, which is why the POSIX toolkit still matters. And for locating binaries and their packages, `command -v`, `which`, `type -a`, `readlink -f` and `dpkg -S`/`rpm -qf` answer different questions — "what will run", "where is it really", and "who put it there".
sections.code:
# ---------- grep ----------
grep -rn --include='*.py' --exclude-dir={.git,node_modules} 'def handle_' src/
grep -c ERROR /var/log/app.log                  # counts LINES, not occurrences
grep -o 'ERROR' /var/log/app.log | wc -l        # counts occurrences
grep -Fq "$needle" file && echo present         # -F: literal; -q: quiet, exit status only
grep -E 'HTTP/1\.[01]" (5[0-9]{2})' access.log  # ERE
grep -P '(?<=user_id=)\d+' app.log -o           # PCRE lookbehind (GNU grep with -P)
grep -A3 -B3 'panic:' /var/log/syslog           # context around the interesting line
zgrep 'timeout' /var/log/nginx/access.log.*.gz  # search rotated+compressed logs

# ---------- find as an expression language ----------
find /var/log -xdev -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -size +10M -print
find /srv -xdev \( -name '*.tmp' -o -name '*.bak' \) -type f -delete
find / -xdev -type d -name node_modules -prune -o -type f -name '*.conf' -print
find . -maxdepth 2 -type f -newermt '2026-03-01' -printf '%T+ %10s %p\n' | sort
find /home -xdev -type f -perm -o+w -printf '%M %u %p\n'    # world-writable files
find /var/lib/app -type f -mmin -15                          # changed in last 15 minutes

# -exec ; forks per file; -exec + batches (use + unless the tool is one-file-at-a-time)
find . -name '*.js' -exec grep -l TODO {} +
time find /usr/share -type f -exec md5sum {} \; >/dev/null    # slow
time find /usr/share -type f -exec md5sum {} +  >/dev/null    # much faster

# ---------- xargs safely ----------
find /tmp -xdev -type f -mtime +3 -print0 | xargs -0 -r rm -f       # NUL-separated + -r
find . -name '*.png' -print0 | xargs -0 -P8 -n20 optipng -quiet     # 8-way parallel batches
printf '%s\n' host1 host2 host3 | xargs -I{} -P3 ssh {} 'uptime'

# WRONG - breaks on any filename containing a space or a newline:
#   find . -type f | xargs rm

# Where does this command really come from?
type -a python3
command -v python3
readlink -f "$(command -v python3)"
dpkg -S "$(readlink -f "$(command -v python3)")"

sections.title: 15. Transforming Text: sed, awk, sort, uniq, cut
sections.content:
Unix text tools all follow the same shape: read a stream line by line, apply a rule, emit a stream. Chaining them is how you answer questions about production data without writing a program, and interviewers use these questions because they show whether you can actually operate a machine.

`sed` is a stream editor built around addresses and commands. The substitution `s/pattern/replacement/flags` covers most real use: `g` replaces every occurrence on the line rather than the first, a number replaces the nth, and `I` matches case-insensitively. Addresses restrict where commands apply: `sed -n '10,20p'` prints lines 10 to 20 (`-n` suppresses the default print), `sed '/^#/d'` deletes comment lines, `sed '/BEGIN/,/END/d'` deletes an inclusive range. `-E` enables extended regex so groups do not need escaping, `&` in the replacement means the whole match, and `\1`, `\2` are capture groups. You may use any delimiter after `s`, so `s|/usr/local|/opt|` avoids escaping every slash when editing paths. In-place editing with `-i` is the flag most likely to hurt you: it is GNU-specific in this form (BSD/macOS `sed` requires an explicit argument, `-i ''`), it creates a new file and renames it over the old one, which breaks hard links and changes the inode, and it happily writes nonsense if your expression is wrong. Always run the expression without `-i` first, and use `-i.bak` when the file matters.

`awk` is a real programming language and is the right tool the moment fields are involved. It splits each input record into fields — `$1`, `$2`, `$NF` for the last, `$0` for the whole line — and runs `pattern { action }` blocks against each record, with `BEGIN` and `END` blocks around the stream. Default field splitting is on runs of whitespace with leading and trailing whitespace ignored, which is exactly what you want for `ps`, `df` and log output; `-F,` or `-F'\t'` switches to a fixed delimiter, and with an explicit delimiter empty fields *are* preserved, which is the important difference from whitespace mode. `NR` is the record number and `NF` the field count. Associative arrays make aggregation trivial, so the entire "top N by count" pattern is one expression, and `printf` gives you formatting. The classic one-liners — sum a column, average a latency field, count status codes per endpoint, print lines where field 5 exceeds a threshold — are worth being able to write without thinking.

`sort` and `uniq` are a pair and the pairing is the point: `uniq` only collapses *adjacent* duplicates, so it is nearly always wrong without a preceding `sort`. `sort -n` is numeric, `-h` understands human suffixes like `4.2G` (perfect for `du` output), `-r` reverses, `-u` deduplicates, `-t` sets a delimiter and `-k` selects a key. `-k` has a trap: `-k2` means "from field 2 to the end of the line", so to sort on field 2 alone you must write `-k2,2`. For large files, `LC_ALL=C sort` is both faster and gives stable byte ordering rather than locale-dependent collation — worth remembering when a script behaves differently on two machines. `uniq -c` prefixes counts, `-d` shows only duplicates, `-u` only uniques.

`cut -d, -f2,5` is fine for strictly single-character-delimited data, but it cannot handle runs of spaces or quoted CSV fields, so `awk` is usually the better answer. Rounding out the kit: `tr` for character-level translation and deletion (`tr -d '\r'` to strip Windows line endings, `tr -s ' '` to squeeze repeats), `head`/`tail` with `tail -f` to follow and `tail -n +2` to skip a header, `wc -l`, `paste`, `join`, `column -t` for readable output, and `jq` whenever the data is JSON — which, for modern logs and APIs, is most of the time.

One buffering detail that wastes hours if you do not know it. C stdio line-buffers when stdout is a terminal but block-buffers when it is a pipe. So `tail -f app.log | grep ERROR` can appear to hang: `grep` has matches, but it is holding them until its buffer fills. `grep --line-buffered`, `awk` with `fflush()`, `sed -u`, or wrapping the producer in `stdbuf -oL` all fix it.
sections.code:
# ---------- awk: the aggregations you will be asked for ----------
# Top 10 client IPs in an nginx access log
awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) printf "%8d %s\n", c[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn | head

# Count responses by status code
awk '{s[$9]++} END {for (k in s) print k, s[k]}' access.log | sort -k2 -rn

# Requests per minute (nginx time field looks like [01/Mar/2026:09:14:22 +0000])
awk '{split($4,t,":"); print t[2]":"t[3]}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Mean and p95 of a latency column ($NF here, in seconds)
awk '{s+=$NF; n++} END {printf "mean=%.3f n=%d\n", s/n, n}' access.log
awk '{print $NF}' access.log | sort -n | awk '{a[NR]=$1} END {print "p95="a[int(NR*0.95)]}'

# Sum a size column, print only rows over a threshold, use a delimiter
awk -F',' '$3 > 1000 {sum += $3; rows++} END {print rows, sum}' data.csv
df -P | awk 'NR>1 && $5+0 > 80 {print $6, $5}'      # filesystems over 80% full

# ---------- sed ----------
sed -n '/ERROR/,/^$/p' app.log                # from each ERROR to the next blank line
sed -E 's/([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}/x.x.x.x/g' access.log   # redact IPv4
sed 's|/usr/local|/opt|g' paths.txt           # alternative delimiter: no slash escaping
sed -i.bak '/^DEBUG/d' /etc/app.conf          # in place, WITH a backup
sed -n '1000,1010p; 1011q' huge.log           # print a window, then quit early

# ---------- sort / uniq ----------
du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail          # -h understands 4.2G
sort -t: -k3,3n /etc/passwd | tail -5               # -k3,3 = field 3 ONLY
sort access.log | uniq -c | sort -rn | head         # uniq needs sorted input
LC_ALL=C sort -u big.txt > deduped.txt              # faster + locale-stable

# ---------- misc ----------
tr -d '\r' < dos.txt > unix.txt
cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd | column -t -s:
tail -n +2 data.csv | wc -l                         # skip the header row
kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.phase!="Running") | .metadata.name'

# Buffering: why `tail -f x | grep y` looks frozen
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR
stdbuf -oL ./chatty_program | awk '{print; fflush()}'

sections.title: 16. Standard Streams, Redirection, Pipelines, and Exit Status
sections.content:
Three descriptors are open when a process starts: 0 (stdin), 1 (stdout), 2 (stderr). Keeping normal output and diagnostics on separate descriptors is what makes composition work — you can pipe a program's results into another program while its errors still reach your terminal. Any script you write should honour the convention: results to stdout, diagnostics and progress to stderr, meaningful exit status.

Redirection rewires those descriptors before the program starts, so the program itself never knows. `>` truncates and writes, `>>` appends, `<` supplies stdin, and `n>&m` makes descriptor n a duplicate of m. The famous gotcha is ordering, because the shell applies redirections strictly left to right. `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` first points stdout at the file, then points stderr at whatever stdout currently is — the file — so both land in `out.txt`. `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt` points stderr at the terminal (where stdout still is at that moment), then moves stdout to the file, so errors go to the terminal and only normal output to the file. Bash's `&>` is the unambiguous shorthand for the first form. `2>/dev/null` discards errors, and using it as a reflex to silence a script is how real failures become invisible.

Beyond the basics: here-documents (`<<EOF`) feed literal text as stdin, and quoting the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) disables variable and command expansion inside — critical when the text contains `$` characters you want preserved, such as an awk program or a password. `<<-EOF` strips leading *tabs* only, so it lets you indent a heredoc inside a function. Here-strings (`<<<"$var"`) feed one string. Process substitution `<(cmd)` presents a command's output as a filename, which is how you `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)` without temp files. `tee` splits a stream to a file and onward, and `tee -a` appends; `command | tee /dev/stderr | next` is a handy debugging tap.

A pipeline connects the stdout of each stage to the stdin of the next — stderr is not piped unless you redirect it — and, importantly, all stages run *concurrently*, not one after another. That is why `tail -f | grep` works at all, and why a pipeline's memory footprint stays small on huge inputs. Two consequences follow. First, when a downstream stage exits early, the upstream one gets `SIGPIPE` on its next write and dies with status 141 — this is a feature, and it is why `head` on a huge file returns instantly, but it also means `set -o pipefail` will report failure for `producer | head -5`, which trips people up. Second, in bash each stage runs in a subshell, so a variable assigned inside `... | while read ...` is lost when the loop ends. The standard fixes are process substitution (`while read ...; done < <(cmd)`) or `shopt -s lastpipe` in a non-interactive shell.

Exit status is the machine-readable half of a program's output: 0 means success, 1-125 are program-defined failures, 126 means found but not executable, 127 means command not found, and 128+N means killed by signal N. A pipeline's status is that of its *last* command by default, which is why `curl bad-url | jq .` reports success — `jq` was perfectly happy processing nothing. `set -o pipefail` changes it to the rightmost non-zero status, and bash's `PIPESTATUS` array holds every stage's status individually if you need to distinguish them. `$?` holds the last status and is fragile: it is overwritten by the very next command, including an `echo` you inserted to debug, so capture it immediately into a variable if you need it twice.

Finally, `&&` and `||` are short-circuit operators on exit status, not boolean logic on output, and the idiom `cmd && echo ok || echo failed` has a subtle bug: if `cmd` succeeds but `echo ok` fails, you get both branches. Prefer a real `if` for anything with consequences.

log INFO "starting"       # never pollutes the caller's data stream

password=$uper$ecret      # quoted delimiter: NO expansion, $ survives literally
EOF

    HostName ${PROD_IP}   # unquoted delimiter: expansion happens
EOF

comm -13 <(sort want.txt) <(sort have.txt)

# Exit status of a pipeline
$ false | true ; echo $?
0                              # status of the LAST stage only
$ set -o pipefail
$ false | true ; echo $?
1                              # rightmost non-zero
$ curl -sf https://api/x | jq -e '.ok' ; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"

# SIGPIPE is normal and useful
$ zcat 40gb.gz | head -3       # decompressor is killed by SIGPIPE (141), not an error

find . -name '*.log' | while read -r f; do count=$((count+1)); done
echo "$count"        # 0  -- the loop ran in a subshell
count=0
while read -r f; do count=$((count+1)); done < <(find . -name '*.log')
echo "$count"        # correct

sections.title: 17. Memory, Swap, and the OOM Killer
sections.content:
The first thing to understand about Linux memory is that "free memory is wasted memory". The kernel uses whatever RAM applications are not using for the page cache — copies of file data — because a cache hit avoids a disk read and the cache can be dropped instantly under pressure. So the `free` column in `free -h` is almost always small on a healthy machine, and reading it as "we are nearly out of memory" is a beginner's mistake. The column that matters is **available**, which is the kernel's own estimate of how much a new workload could obtain without swapping, counting reclaimable page cache and slab. `buff/cache` is largely reclaimable; `shared` includes tmpfs, and tmpfs is *not* reclaimable — files in `/dev/shm` or `/tmp` on tmpfs occupy RAM until deleted, which is a genuinely sneaky way to run a machine out of memory.

Per-process, the number people quote is RSS (resident set size): pages currently in physical RAM. VSZ (virtual size) is address space reserved, which includes memory-mapped files and untouched allocations and is nearly meaningless as a pressure metric — a Java process routinely shows tens of gigabytes of VSZ. RSS has its own distortion: shared pages, including shared libraries and copy-on-write pages after a fork, are counted in full against every process, so summing RSS across a process tree double-counts badly. `PSS` in `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` divides shared pages fairly among sharers and is the honest number when you need one.

Linux also *overcommits*: `malloc` can succeed for more memory than physically exists, because programs routinely reserve more than they touch and the kernel only allocates physical pages on first write. The policy is `vm.overcommit_memory` (0 = heuristic, the default; 1 = always allow; 2 = strict accounting against a ratio). The consequence is that allocation failures often do not appear as a failed `malloc` at all; instead the machine runs out of physical pages later, when the memory is actually touched, and something must die.

That something is chosen by the **OOM killer**. When the kernel cannot reclaim enough, it scores every process — roughly proportional to memory used, adjusted by `oom_score_adj` (-1000 to 1000, where -1000 makes a process exempt) — and kills the highest scorer, logging `Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (java) total-vm:... anon-rss:...` to the kernel ring buffer. Note the sharp edge: the biggest process is usually your main application, so the database gets killed to save the machine. Two things follow for an interview answer. First, `dmesg -T | grep -i 'out of memory'` or `journalctl -k -g 'Out of memory'` is how you *confirm* an OOM kill rather than guessing, and the log line names the victim and its RSS at death. Second, an OOM kill is SIGKILL, so the process gets no chance to flush or clean up, and its exit status is 137.

Cgroups change the scope. With cgroup v2 a service or container gets `memory.max` (a hard limit — exceed it and the kernel OOM-kills a process *inside that cgroup*, leaving the rest of the machine alone) and `memory.high` (a throttling threshold — the kernel aggressively reclaims and stalls the cgroup rather than killing). This is exactly what a Kubernetes memory limit becomes, which is why an `OOMKilled` container shows exit code 137 while the node itself was fine. `memory.events` in the cgroup directory has an `oom_kill` counter, and `systemctl status` or `systemd-cgtop` shows per-unit usage.

Swap is the last piece and is widely misunderstood. Swap does not make a machine slower by existing; it lets the kernel evict genuinely cold anonymous pages so that hot pages and cache keep the RAM, which usually improves behaviour. What is catastrophic is *thrashing*: when the working set exceeds RAM, pages are read back almost as soon as they are written out, the machine becomes I/O bound, latency explodes, and it often stays technically alive but useless — arguably worse than a quick OOM kill and restart. `vm.swappiness` (default 60) biases the reclaim choice between anonymous pages and page cache; lowering it to 10 is common on database servers. The diagnostic to watch is not "how much swap is used" but the *rate*: sustained non-zero `si`/`so` columns in `vmstat 1` mean active swapping right now. Kubernetes historically required swap to be disabled on nodes because the scheduler's memory accounting assumed it was off; more recent versions have opt-in support, but "swap off on nodes" remains the common configuration.

# What the numbers actually mean
$ free -h
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            31Gi        18Gi       0.6Gi       1.2Gi        12Gi        11Gi
#                                       ^^^^^ ignore this      ^^^^^^^^^^ this is the number
# shared 1.2Gi = tmpfs (/dev/shm, /run, maybe /tmp) - NOT reclaimable

# Per-process truth
ps -eo pid,ppid,rss,vsz,comm --sort=-rss | head        # RSS, not VSZ
grep -E '^(Rss|Pss|Swap):' /proc/1873/smaps_rollup     # PSS: shared pages divided fairly
systemd-cgtop -m                                       # memory by unit/slice

# Confirm an OOM kill instead of guessing
dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|oom-kill|killed process'
journalctl -k -b -g 'Out of memory'
# Out of memory: Killed process 24413 (java) total-vm:9812340kB, anon-rss:7810244kB ...
# -> victim, its RSS at death, and which cgroup it was in

# Is it swapping RIGHT NOW? (rate matters, not the total)
vmstat 1 5
# procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
#  r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
#  4  3 812344  61232  10240 214400  912  1480  4210  980 5120 9800 12  9  6 73  0
#                                    ^^^  ^^^^ sustained non-zero = thrashing

# Protect / sacrifice specific processes
choom -p 1873 -n -500              # lower oom_score_adj: less likely to be picked
echo 1000 > /proc/4711/oom_score_adj   # sacrificial: kill this one first
# systemd unit equivalent:
#   [Service]
#   OOMScoreAdjust=-500
#   MemoryMax=2G          # hard cap: cgroup OOM kills inside this unit only
#   MemoryHigh=1500M      # throttle+reclaim before that point

# cgroup v2 accounting for a unit
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/checkout-api.service/memory.current
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/checkout-api.service/memory.max
grep oom /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/checkout-api.service/memory.events

sysctl vm.swappiness vm.overcommit_memory vm.overcommit_ratio

sections.title: 18. Performance Triage: load, top, vmstat, iostat, ss, lsof
sections.content:
"The server is slow" is the most common real-world prompt and the most common interview scenario, and what is being assessed is method, not command recall. The useful frame is the USE method: for every resource — CPU, memory, disk, network — check **U**tilisation (how busy), **S**aturation (how much queued work is waiting), and **E**rrors. Saturation is the part people skip, and it is usually where the answer lives, because a resource at 100% utilisation with no queue is merely busy, while one at 70% with a growing queue is broken.

Start with **load average** and understand what it actually measures on Linux, because it is different from other Unixes: it is an exponentially damped average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes of the number of tasks that are either runnable *or* in uninterruptible sleep (`D` state, essentially blocked on I/O). Including D state is why a load of 40 on an 8-core box can coexist with 95% idle CPU — the tasks are queued on a saturated or failing disk, or on a hung NFS mount, not on the CPU. So load must always be read against core count (`nproc`) and alongside the CPU breakdown. Comparing the 1, 5 and 15 minute figures tells you the direction: rising or already receding.

Next, `top` (or `htop`) for the CPU-time breakdown, where each column implies a different investigation. High `us` means application code — profile it. High `sy` means kernel time, typically syscall or context-switch storms. High `wa` (I/O wait) points at storage. `si`/`hi` are soft/hard interrupts, often network on a busy host. And `st`, steal time, is CPU the hypervisor gave to another tenant: nonzero steal on a cloud VM means the host is oversubscribed and the fix is a different instance, not your code. Press `1` to see per-CPU rows, which distinguishes "one saturated core" — a single-threaded bottleneck or interrupts pinned to CPU0 — from an evenly loaded machine, and `H` to see individual threads.

Then move to the per-resource tools. `vmstat 1` is the best single overview: `r` is the run queue (compare against core count for CPU saturation), `b` is processes blocked on I/O, `si`/`so` reveal swapping, `bi`/`bo` are block I/O, `cs` and `in` are context switches and interrupts, and the CPU columns repeat the top breakdown. `iostat -xz 1` covers disks: `r/s` and `w/s` for IOPS, throughput, `await` for average latency in milliseconds — the metric an application actually feels — and `aqu-sz` for queue depth, which is the saturation signal. Treat `%util` carefully: it means "time with at least one request in flight", which was a valid saturation proxy for a single spinning disk but is misleading for an SSD or NVMe device that serves many requests in parallel, where 100% `%util` can be perfectly healthy. Remember that the *first* report from `vmstat`, `iostat` and `sar` is an average since boot; always take the second and later samples.

For the network and for "who is holding this", `ss` has replaced `netstat` and is far faster on busy hosts. `ss -ltnp` lists listening TCP sockets with the owning process, `ss -tanp state established` shows established connections, `ss -s` gives a socket summary, and `ss -ti` exposes per-connection TCP internals including RTT, congestion window and retransmits. One detail interviewers love: on a *listening* socket, `Recv-Q` is the current number of completed connections waiting to be accepted and `Send-Q` is the configured backlog maximum, so a nonzero Recv-Q means your application is not calling `accept()` fast enough and clients are about to see connection failures. `lsof` answers ownership questions — `lsof -nP -i :8080`, `lsof -p PID`, `lsof +D /var/lib/data`, `lsof +L1` for unlinked files — and `fuser -v /mnt/x` is the quick way to find who is keeping a filesystem busy so it will not unmount.

Two more layers before you escalate. `dmesg -T` (or `journalctl -k`) surfaces hardware and kernel-level events that never reach application logs: OOM kills, segfaults, EXT4 errors, NIC resets, "TCP: out of memory". And the Pressure Stall Information files under `/proc/pressure/` are the most direct saturation metric the kernel offers — `some avg10` for cpu, io and memory tells you the percentage of the last ten seconds during which at least one task was stalled waiting for that resource. When you need to know *what a specific process is doing*, `strace -f -p PID -c` summarises its syscalls (with a heavy slowdown, so never on a hot production process without thought), `perf top` shows where CPU time is going kernel-wide, and `pidstat 1` breaks usage down per process over time.

# ---------- the 60-second triage, in order ----------
uptime                        # load 1/5/15 vs nproc; rising or falling?
nproc
dmesg -T | tail -30           # OOM, segfault, EXT4 errors, NIC resets, TCP OOM
vmstat 1 5                    # r, b, si/so, bi/bo, cs, and the cpu split (IGNORE line 1)
mpstat -P ALL 1 3             # is it ONE hot core or all of them?
pidstat 1 3                   # which process is burning the CPU
iostat -xz 1 3                # await + aqu-sz per device (IGNORE the first report)
free -h                       # look at "available", not "free"
ss -s                         # socket summary: TCP established / timewait / orphans
top -b -n1 -o %CPU | head -20

# Reading top's CPU line
# %Cpu(s):  12.1 us,  9.4 sy,  0.0 ni, 5.2 id, 72.4 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.9 si, 0.0 st
#   us app code | sy kernel | wa blocked on I/O | si softirq (network)
#   st = STEAL: the hypervisor gave your CPU to someone else -> noisy neighbour

# Disk: await is what the application feels; aqu-sz is saturation
iostat -xz 1
# Device  r/s   w/s  rkB/s  wkB/s  r_await w_await aqu-sz %util
# nvme0n1 120  3400   4800 210000    0.42    38.10  14.20  99.8
#                                            ^^^^^ 38ms writes with a queue of 14 = saturated
pidstat -d 1                  # per-process disk I/O
iotop -oPa                    # accumulated I/O by process, if installed

# Sockets and ports
ss -ltnp                                   # listening TCP + owning process (needs root)
ss -tanp state established '( dport = :5432 )'
ss -ti dst 10.0.3.7 | head                 # rtt, cwnd, retrans for a specific peer
ss -ltn                                    # Recv-Q on a LISTEN socket = unaccepted backlog
nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops TcpRetransSegs

# Who is holding this file / port / mount?
lsof -nP -i :8080
lsof -p 1873
fuser -vm /mnt/data                        # why won't this unmount?

# Kernel-level saturation, straight from PSI
cat /proc/pressure/cpu /proc/pressure/io /proc/pressure/memory
# some avg10=64.11 -> for 64% of the last 10s, at least one task was stalled on this resource

# Drill into one process
strace -f -p 1873 -c              # syscall summary (slows the target - use deliberately)
strace -f -p 1873 -e trace=openat,connect -s 200
perf top -p 1873
cat /proc/1873/wchan; echo       # what a D-state process is blocked in

sections.title: 19. Shell Scripting That Does Not Betray You: set -euo pipefail, trap, quoting
sections.content:
A shell script that runs in production is production code, and the shell's defaults are hostile to that. By default a script continues merrily after any command fails, treats a typo'd variable as an empty string, and reports success for a pipeline whose first stage exploded. The conventional first line of defence is `set -euo pipefail`, and a strong candidate can explain each flag *and* its failure modes rather than reciting it as a charm.

`set -e` (errexit) exits when a command returns non-zero. Its exceptions are extensive and you must know them: it does not fire for a command whose status is being *tested* — anything in an `if` or `while` condition, anything preceding `&&` or `||` (except the final command of such a list), or a command negated with `!`. Crucially, when a shell *function* is invoked in one of those contexts, errexit is suppressed for everything inside it too, which is how a "checked" helper function silently swallows failures. The single nastiest interaction is with `local` and `export`: `local out=$(failing_cmd)` never triggers errexit, because the exit status observed is that of `local` itself, which succeeded. Always split the declaration: `local out; out=$(failing_cmd)`. And when a command is *allowed* to fail, say so explicitly with `|| true`, so the intent is visible.

`set -u` (nounset) turns a reference to an unset variable into an immediate error, which catches the classic `rm -rf "$PREFIX/"` disaster where `PREFIX` was never set. Use `${VAR:-default}` for optional values and `${VAR:?message}` to fail with a clear message for required ones. Under bash versions older than 4.4, `"${arr[@]}"` on an empty array counts as unset, so scripts that must run on older systems write `"${arr[@]+"${arr[@]}"}"`.

`set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline return the rightmost non-zero status instead of only the last command's, turning `curl bad | jq .` from a silent success into a detected failure. Its own trap is `SIGPIPE`: a producer killed because a consumer such as `head` exited early returns 141, and pipefail dutifully reports that as an error. Wrap those cases (`{ producer || true; } | head`).

Beyond the three flags, the habits that keep scripts safe are consistent. Quote every expansion — `"$var"`, `"$@"`, `"${array[@]}"` — because unquoted expansions undergo word splitting and globbing, which is why paths with spaces break scripts and why `$*` is almost never what you want. Use `trap cleanup EXIT` together with `mktemp -d` so temporary state disappears on every exit path including errors and signals; add `trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR` (with `set -E` so it propagates into functions) for a usable error message. Guard against concurrent runs with `flock` on a dedicated descriptor. Prefer `[[ ]]` over `[ ]` in bash for safer comparisons, and remember `[[ ]]`, arrays and `local` do not exist in POSIX `sh` — so if your shebang is `#!/bin/sh`, on Debian and in most containers that is `dash`, not bash, and your script will break in ways that only appear on the target system.

Two design points elevate an answer. **Idempotency**: a script that may be retried must produce the same end state when run twice, which means checking before creating, using `mkdir -p`, writing to a temp file and `mv`-ing it into place (rename is atomic within a filesystem, so no reader ever sees a half-written config), and making deletes tolerate a missing target. **Observability**: log to stderr with timestamps, echo the commands you are about to run when a `--verbose` or `set -x` flag is set (`PS4` can be customised to include line numbers), support `--dry-run` for anything destructive, and exit with distinct non-zero statuses for distinct failure classes so a caller can react. Finally, run `shellcheck` in CI. It catches unquoted expansions, useless `cat`, `[ $x = y ]` bugs, and a long list of subtle portability issues, and it is the cheapest quality improvement available for shell code.

And know the ceiling: once a script needs data structures, real error handling, retries with backoff, or unit tests, it has outgrown the shell. The right answer to "would you write this in bash?" is sometimes no.
sections.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# A production-shaped script: strict mode, cleanup, locking, idempotence, logging.
set -Eeuo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'                       # stop word-splitting on spaces (know why you did this)

readonly SCRIPT_NAME=${0##*/}
readonly LOCK_FILE=/run/lock/${SCRIPT_NAME}.lock
: "${TARGET_DIR:?TARGET_DIR must be set}"        # required input, fails loudly
readonly DRY_RUN=${DRY_RUN:-0}                   # optional input, sane default

log()  { printf '%s %-5s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$1" "${*:2}" >&2; }
die()  { log ERROR "$*"; exit 1; }
run()  { if (( DRY_RUN )); then log DRY "$*"; else log RUN "$*"; "$@"; fi; }

# One instance only. fd 9 is released automatically when the process exits.
exec 9>"$LOCK_FILE"
flock -n 9 || { log WARN "another run holds the lock; exiting"; exit 0; }

# Cleanup on EVERY exit path: success, error, or signal.
TMPDIR_LOCAL=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() { rm -rf -- "$TMPDIR_LOCAL"; }
trap cleanup EXIT
trap 'die "line $LINENO: command failed: $BASH_COMMAND"' ERR    # needs set -E

main() {
  local out                       # NEVER `local out=$(cmd)` - it hides the exit status
  out=$(curl -fsS --max-time 10 "https://api.internal/manifest.json")

  mkdir -p -- "$TARGET_DIR"       # idempotent
  # Atomic publish: write beside the target, then rename. Readers never see a partial file.
  printf '%s\n' "$out" > "$TMPDIR_LOCAL/manifest.json"
  run mv -f -- "$TMPDIR_LOCAL/manifest.json" "$TARGET_DIR/manifest.json"

  local -a stale=()
  while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do stale+=("$f"); done \
    < <(find "$TARGET_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.tmp' -mtime +1 -print0)
  (( ${#stale[@]} )) && run rm -f -- "${stale[@]}"

  log INFO "done (${#stale[@]} stale files removed)"
}

main "$@"
# ------------------------------------------------------------------
# set -e does NOT fire in any of these contexts:
if failing_cmd; then :; fi            # tested -> no exit
failing_cmd || handle_it              # left of || -> no exit
! failing_cmd                         # negated  -> no exit
check() { failing_cmd; more_stuff; }  # ...and inside a function called that way, too
if check; then :; fi                  # errexit is suppressed for the WHOLE function body

local x=$(false); echo $?             # 0  <-- `local` succeeded; the failure vanished
local x; x=$(false); echo $?          # 1  <-- correct

# Quoting
cp $src $dst                          # breaks on "my file.txt"; globs; splits
cp -- "$src" "$dst"                   # correct ("--" protects against leading dashes)
for a in "$@"; do ...; done           # each argument preserved
for a in $*;  do ...; done            # re-split and globbed - almost always wrong

# Debugging and CI
PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE##*/}:${LINENO}: ' bash -x ./deploy.sh
shellcheck -S warning ./deploy.sh
bash -n ./deploy.sh                   # syntax check without executing

interviewQA.q: df says the root filesystem is 100% full, but du -sh / only adds up to about half the disk. What is going on and how do you find it?
interviewQA.a:
They are measuring different things. `df` reads the filesystem's own free-block counters out of the superblock, so it counts every allocated block whether or not anything can reach it. `du` walks the directory tree and sums the blocks of files it can *reach*. Anything allocated but unreachable shows up in `df` and is invisible to `du`.

There are four realistic causes, and I would check them in this order. First, a deleted-but-still-open file: someone ran `rm` on a large log while a process had it open, so the directory entry is gone but the inode's blocks stay allocated until the last file descriptor closes. `lsof -nP +L1` lists exactly those. The clean fix is to make the process reopen its logs (`kill -USR1` for nginx, or restart the service); the emergency fix is `truncate -s 0 /proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`, which reclaims the space instantly without touching the process. Second, files hidden underneath a mount point: data was written to a directory before a disk was mounted over it, so `du` cannot see it while the blocks are still consumed. `mount --bind / /mnt/underlay` and look there. Third, ext4's reserved blocks — 5% by default for root — which `df` excludes from Avail, so Use% can read 100% while gigabytes remain; `tune2fs -m 1` recovers most of that on a data volume. Fourth, `du` undercounts sparse files (it reports allocated, not apparent, size) and counts hard-linked files only once.

I would also immediately check `df -i`, because inode exhaustion produces the same `ENOSPC` error from the application while `df -h` looks fine — and always run `du` with `-x` so it does not cross into `/proc`, `/sys` or a network mount and give me nonsense.
followUps: You find a 40 GB deleted file held open by a process you must not restart. What do you do?
Why does truncating through /proc/PID/fd work when deleting the file did not?
How would you prevent this class of incident structurally?
df -i is at 100% on ext4. What are your options?

interviewQA.q: Explain the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link.
interviewQA.a:
A file on disk is an inode: metadata plus pointers to data blocks. The name is not part of the inode — names live in directories as (name, inode number) pairs. A hard link is simply a second directory entry pointing at the same inode, which increments the inode's link count. There is no original and no copy; the two names are completely equal, and removing one just decrements the count. The data is freed only when the count reaches zero *and* no process holds the file open.

A symbolic link is a different inode whose contents are a path string, resolved fresh on every access. That gives it the opposite properties. Hard links cannot cross filesystems, because inode numbers are only meaningful within one filesystem, and the kernel forbids hard links to directories because they would create cycles that tree-walking tools could not handle. Symlinks can cross filesystems, can point at a path that does not exist yet, and break silently if you move or delete the target. Symlink permission bits are ignored on Linux — the target's permissions are what get checked.

Practically: `ls -li` shows the inode number and link count so you can tell them apart at a glance. Hard links are how backup tools such as rsync's `--link-dest` make daily snapshots that share unchanged files, so a hundred snapshots cost one copy of the data. Symlinks are what you use for `current -> releases/2026-03-01`, because you can atomically repoint a deployment with `ln -sfn` plus `mv`. And the deleted-but-open-file phenomenon is the same link-count mechanism seen from the other side: an open descriptor is an extra reference the directory tree cannot see.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through what happens when you type `ls -l /tmp` at a bash prompt and press Enter.
interviewQA.a:
Bash reads the line, performs expansions (alias, brace, tilde, parameter, command substitution, then word splitting and globbing) and produces the argument vector `["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]`. It checks whether `ls` is a function or builtin; it is neither, so it searches each directory in `$PATH` in order for an executable file called `ls`, using its hash table to skip the search if it has resolved it before.

Then it calls `fork()`, which creates a child that is a copy-on-write clone of the shell. In the child, and only in the child, the shell applies whatever setup this command needs: any redirections via `dup2`, resetting signal dispositions the shell had ignored, putting the process into a new process group and making it the foreground group of the terminal. Then it calls `execve("/usr/bin/ls", argv, envp)`, which replaces the child's address space with the new program. The kernel maps the ELF image, sees the `PT_INTERP` header and loads the dynamic linker `ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which maps `libc` and any other shared libraries, applies relocations, and finally jumps to `_start` and then `main`.

`ls` calls `openat`/`getdents64` to read the directory, `statx` on each entry for the `-l` metadata, `getpwuid`/`getgrgid` (through NSS) to turn UIDs and GIDs into names, and writes the formatted output to file descriptor 1 — which is the terminal, so libc line-buffers it. On exit it calls `exit_group`, and the kernel sends SIGCHLD to bash, which was blocked in `waitpid`. Bash collects the exit status into `$?`, takes back the terminal foreground group, and prints the prompt.

The two details worth calling out are that `fork` plus `exec` exist as separate calls precisely so the shell can configure the child in between, and that the kernel enforces permissions at `execve` and at each `openat`, checking the traverse bit on every directory in the path.

interviewQA.q: SIGTERM versus SIGKILL: what is the difference, and why can't you catch SIGKILL?
interviewQA.a:
SIGTERM (15) is a request to terminate that the process can catch. A well-behaved server installs a handler and uses it to stop accepting new connections, drain in-flight requests, flush buffers and close database connections, deregister from service discovery, remove its PID file, and exit with a clean status. SIGKILL (9) is not delivered to the process at all in a meaningful sense — the kernel simply removes it. No handler runs, no destructors, no flush, no unlink of temp or lock files.

SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are uncatchable by design, because they are the operator's guaranteed last resort. If a process could trap SIGKILL, a buggy or malicious program could make itself unkillable, and the kernel would have no way to reclaim resources.

The operational consequence is that SIGKILL should be the escalation, never the default. `kill -9` as a habit is how you get corrupted state, stale lock files, dropped connections during deploys, and databases that need recovery on start. The correct pattern is TERM, wait a bounded time, then KILL — which is exactly what systemd does (`KillSignal=SIGTERM`, wait `TimeoutStopSec=`, default 90 s, then SIGKILL) and what `docker stop` and Kubernetes do with their grace periods. If a service is regularly being SIGKILLed at the end of a deploy, the grace period is shorter than its real drain time, and that is a configuration bug worth fixing.

Two edges worth mentioning. A process in `D` state — uninterruptible sleep inside a kernel I/O path — will not die even from SIGKILL until that I/O completes or errors, which is why a hung NFS mount produces unkillable processes. And PID 1 is special: the kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1 for signals it has not explicitly handled, so a containerised app with no SIGTERM handler ignores `docker stop` entirely and always ends up hard-killed.

interviewQA.q: What does `set -euo pipefail` do, and where does each part let you down?
interviewQA.a:
`set -e` exits the script when a command returns non-zero. `set -u` makes referencing an unset variable a fatal error. `set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline return the rightmost non-zero exit status instead of only the last command's. Together they convert the shell's default "carry on regardless" into fail-fast behaviour.

Each has real caveats. `set -e` does not fire for any command whose status is being tested: inside an `if` or `while` condition, to the left of `&&` or `||`, or after `!`. More subtly, when a *function* is called in one of those contexts, errexit is disabled for the whole function body, so failures inside a "checked" helper vanish. The nastiest case is `local x=$(cmd)` or `export x=$(cmd)`: the exit status observed is that of `local`/`export`, which succeeded, so the failure is silently discarded. Always write `local x; x=$(cmd)`.

`set -u` breaks on legitimately optional variables, so you need `${VAR:-default}` for optional values and `${VAR:?message}` for required ones; and on bash older than 4.4, expanding an empty array as `"${arr[@]}"` counts as unset.

`pipefail` interacts badly with SIGPIPE. `zcat huge.gz | head -3` kills `zcat` with SIGPIPE, which is normal and desirable, but it exits 141 and pipefail reports the pipeline as failed. Wrap those deliberately: `{ zcat huge.gz || true; } | head -3`.

So I use `set -Eeuo pipefail` (the `-E` makes an `ERR` trap propagate into functions) as a baseline, but I treat it as a safety net rather than error handling. Anything allowed to fail gets an explicit `|| true`, anything that must be handled gets a real `if`, and I run `shellcheck` in CI because it catches most of these patterns statically.

interviewQA.q: A systemd service keeps restarting. Walk me through debugging it.
interviewQA.a:
First I read the unit's own summary: `systemctl status foo` gives the load state, the active state and substate, the main PID and exit status, the cgroup with every process still in it, and the last few journal lines. The exit status is the first real signal — 0 with `Restart=always` means the process is exiting cleanly and being restarted; 203 is `EXEC` failure meaning the binary path is wrong or not executable; 200-series statuses generally mean systemd could not set the service up (bad user, missing directory, a namespace directive that failed).

Then `journalctl -u foo -b --no-pager`, and if it is crash-looping, `journalctl -u foo -f` in one window while I restart in another. I look at whether it fails immediately or after some seconds — an instant failure is usually configuration, permissions or a missing dependency, while a delayed one is usually the application dying on real work.

Common causes in the order I find them: a config file the service user cannot read (check with `sudo -u svcuser cat`), a port already in use (`ss -ltnp`), a dependency not actually ready because the unit uses `Requires=` without `After=`, or `Type=simple` where the dependent thing had not finished starting; a missing state directory (`StateDirectory=` or `RuntimeDirectory=` is the correct fix, not `mkdir` in a script); an environment variable present in my shell but absent under systemd, which sources nothing; a sandboxing directive such as `ProtectSystem=strict` blocking a write path (`ReadWritePaths=` fixes it); and getting OOM-killed, which shows as status `killed, signal=KILL` plus a matching `dmesg -T | grep -i 'out of memory'` line.

Two things always worth checking: `systemctl cat foo` to see the merged unit including drop-ins, because the file I am reading is often not the file in effect; and if the restarts have *stopped*, `systemctl status` saying "start request repeated too quickly" means the rate limiter (`StartLimitBurst` within `StartLimitIntervalSec`) has latched the unit into failed state, which needs `systemctl reset-failed` after the fix. To iterate quickly I run the exact `ExecStart` by hand as the service user with the same environment, or use `systemd-run --uid=svcuser --pty` to reproduce it under the same constraints.
followUps: The unit stopped restarting altogether. Why, and how do you clear it?
It works when you run the command manually as root but not under systemd. What do you check?

Where do you put your changes so a package upgrade doesn't overwrite them?

interviewQA.q: Load average is 40 on an 8-core machine, but top shows the CPU is 90% idle. Explain.
interviewQA.a:
Linux's load average is not a CPU metric. It is an exponentially damped average of the number of tasks that are runnable *or* in uninterruptible sleep — `D` state — which on Linux essentially means blocked in the kernel waiting on I/O. Other Unixes count only runnable tasks; Linux deliberately includes D state so that load reflects overall demand on the system, not just the CPU.

So a load of 40 with an idle CPU means roughly 40 tasks are queued waiting for something that is not the processor. In practice that is nearly always storage or a network filesystem: a saturated or failing disk, a RAID array rebuilding, an NFS or FUSE mount whose server is unreachable (which produces processes that cannot even be killed), or a dm-crypt/loopback layer that has stalled. The corroborating evidence is high `wa` in `top`, a nonzero `b` column in `vmstat 1`, and `iostat -xz 1` showing large `await` values with a deep `aqu-sz`. To identify the culprits directly, `ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:32,comm | awk '$2 ~ /D/'` lists the blocked processes and the kernel function each is stuck in, which usually names the subsystem outright.

I would also confirm it is not something more mundane: `dmesg -T` for I/O errors, controller resets or an NFS server "not responding" message, and `/proc/pressure/io` for the kernel's own stall percentage, which is the cleanest single number for I/O saturation.

The general lesson I would state is that load average alone is close to useless without context. It has to be read against core count, alongside the CPU breakdown, and with the knowledge that D-state tasks inflate it. The 1-, 5- and 15-minute values also tell you direction — a 1-minute value well above the 15-minute one means the problem is arriving right now, not receding.

interviewQA.q: How does SSH public key authentication work? Be precise about what is sent over the wire.
interviewQA.a:
It happens in two distinct phases, and the first one is the part candidates usually skip.

Phase one authenticates the *server* and establishes encryption. After the version banner exchange, both sides run a key exchange — typically ECDH over Curve25519 — producing a shared secret that was never transmitted. The server signs the exchange transcript with its host key and sends the corresponding host public key; the client checks that against `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. On the first connection there is nothing to compare, so the client shows the fingerprint and asks — trust on first use — and from then on a change produces the loud host key warning. Everything after this point is encrypted and integrity-protected.

Phase two authenticates the *user*, inside that channel. The client offers a public key. The server looks for a matching line in the target account's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`; if there is none, it rejects immediately and the client tries the next key or method. If there is a match, the server sends a challenge, and the client signs data that includes the unique session identifier from phase one, using the private key. The server verifies the signature with the public key it already holds.

So what crosses the wire is: the client's public key, and a signature. The private key never leaves the client — which is why `ssh-copy-id` only ever transfers a `.pub` file, and why an agent can hold the key while the signing happens locally. Because the signed data is bound to the session identifier, a captured signature cannot be replayed on another connection, and a malicious server cannot reuse your signature to log in elsewhere as you.

In production the operational points are that `authorized_keys` is the access control list and therefore a target — anyone who can write to it grants themselves permanent access — that sshd's `StrictModes` refuses group- or world-writable `~`, `~/.ssh` or `authorized_keys` (the usual cause of "it keeps prompting for a password"), and that at scale SSH certificates are better than distributing keys, because they expire, can carry principals and options, and remove the trust-on-first-use problem for host keys.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between Requires= and After= in a systemd unit?
interviewQA.a:
They are orthogonal, which is exactly why they get confused. `Requires=` is a *requirement* relationship: it declares that the other unit must be started if this one is, and if that unit fails to start or is later stopped, this unit is stopped too. `After=` is purely an *ordering* relationship: if both units happen to be starting in the same transaction, this one is not started until the other has finished starting.

Neither implies the other. `Requires=postgresql.service` on its own will pull PostgreSQL in, but systemd may start both simultaneously and your service will race the database. `After=postgresql.service` on its own means "if postgres is being started too, wait for it" — but nothing pulls it in, so if it is not enabled, your service starts happily without it. Almost always you want both.

The related directives round out the picture: `Wants=` is the soft version of `Requires=` — pull it in, but do not fail if it does not come up — and it is the default choice for loosely coupled dependencies, because a hard `Requires=` propagates failure and can cascade a whole boot. `BindsTo=` is stricter than `Requires=`: if the other unit stops for *any* reason, including the underlying device disappearing, this unit stops too, which suits units tied to a `.device` or `.mount`. `Requisite=` fails immediately if the other unit is not already active rather than starting it. `PartOf=` propagates stop and restart downward, which is how you group a set of services under one target.

The subtlety worth raising unprompted is what "finished starting" means, since that depends on `Type=`. With `Type=simple`, the unit counts as started the moment the process is forked, so `After=` only guarantees the process exists, not that it is listening or ready. If ordering must mean readiness, you need `Type=notify` with `sd_notify(READY=1)`, socket activation, or an explicit readiness check in `ExecStartPre`. And `network-online.target` is the classic example: it requires `Wants=` plus `After=` *and* an enabled `NetworkManager-wait-online`-style unit to mean anything at all.

interviewQA.q: A cron job runs fine when you execute it by hand but fails or does nothing from cron. How do you debug it?
interviewQA.a:
Almost always it is the environment. cron does not source `/etc/profile`, `~/.bashrc` or `~/.profile`, so the job runs with a minimal `PATH` (typically `/usr/bin:/bin`), `SHELL=/bin/sh` rather than bash, `HOME` from the passwd entry, no locale, no `TERM`, and none of the variables your interactive session accumulated — `JAVA_HOME`, a virtualenv on the path, `AWS_PROFILE`, `KUBECONFIG`. There is also no TTY, so anything that prompts, or that runs `ssh` without `-n`, or that expects a terminal, misbehaves. And the working directory is `$HOME`, not wherever you happened to be standing.

My debugging sequence: first confirm cron even tried, with `journalctl -u cron -S today` (or `/var/log/syslog`), because a syntax error or a missing newline at the end of the crontab means the entry never ran. Then reproduce the environment rather than guessing — `env -i /bin/sh -c '/path/to/job.sh'` runs it with an empty environment, and I add variables back until it works. Then I capture output properly: cron mails stdout and stderr to `MAILTO`, and on a box with no MTA that mail is silently discarded, which is how jobs fail unnoticed for months. Redirecting to a log file with `>> /var/log/job.log 2>&1` makes the failure visible.

The fixes are all about making the job self-contained: absolute paths to every binary, an explicit `PATH=` at the top of the crontab, source any environment from a file inside the script, `cd` explicitly, and never depend on the invoking user's shell setup. I also watch for the crontab-specific `%` rule — an unescaped `%` becomes a newline and everything after the first one is fed to the command's stdin, so `date +%F` must be written `date +\%F`. And for anything that could overlap, wrap it in `flock`.

For anything important I would move it to a systemd timer, because then the job is a normal unit: real logs in the journal, a real exit status, `systemctl status`, resource limits, no environment surprises, `Persistent=true` to catch up missed runs, and `RandomizedDelaySec=` to avoid a whole fleet firing at once.

interviewQA.q: Explain umask, and what mode a file and a directory get with umask 027.
interviewQA.a:
`umask` is a per-process mask of permission bits to *withhold* at file creation time. The kernel starts a new regular file from mode `0666` and a new directory from `0777`, then clears every bit set in the umask. Files never get the execute bit at creation — a compiler or `install` has to add it explicitly afterwards.

With umask 027: files get `0666 & ~027 = 0640`, so owner read/write, group read, nothing for others. Directories get `0777 & ~027 = 0750`, so owner full access, group can list and traverse, others get nothing. With the more common default of 022 you get 644 and 755.

The parts people miss are operational. umask is a process attribute inherited across `fork`, so setting it in your shell affects that shell's descendants and nothing else — it is not a system-wide setting and it cannot retroactively change existing files. That means the umask under which a daemon writes files is whatever its *service manager* had, not whatever `/etc/profile` sets for interactive logins. Under systemd the correct place is `UMask=` in the unit, and the default there is 0022. Under cron it is whatever cron's default is, so a job writing files with unexpectedly loose modes usually needs `umask 027` set explicitly at the top of the script.

Also worth knowing: umask only subtracts, so it can tighten defaults but never grant a permission the creating program did not request; a program that explicitly calls `chmod` or `open(..., 0600)` overrides the intent either way. And for directory trees where group access must be reliable, umask is not enough — you want the setgid bit on the directory so group ownership is inherited, and ACLs (`setfacl -d`) if you need per-user defaults.

interviewQA.q: What is a setuid binary, why is it dangerous, and why doesn't setuid work on shell scripts?
interviewQA.a:
A setuid binary runs with the effective UID of the file's owner rather than the caller's, which is how an unprivileged user can perform a specific privileged action. `/usr/bin/passwd` is the canonical example: it is owned by root with the setuid bit, so an ordinary user running it gets a process with root's effective UID that can update `/etc/shadow`, a file they cannot even read.

It is dangerous because the attacker controls almost everything about the process that is about to become root: argv, the environment, resource limits, the working directory, inherited file descriptors, and the terminal. Any bug in argument or input parsing becomes privilege escalation, and historically that is exactly what happened — buffer overflows in argument handling, `LD_PRELOAD` and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` injection (the dynamic loader now ignores those for setuid binaries), `PATH` manipulation when the binary shells out, and resource-limit tricks that force a failure path. Every setuid-root binary on a host is part of the attack surface, which is why `find / -xdev -perm /6000 -type f` belongs in a hardening audit and why `nosuid` is a standard mount option for `/tmp`, `/home` and removable media.

The Linux kernel ignores setuid on interpreted scripts because it cannot be made safe. Running a script means the kernel reads the shebang and executes the *interpreter* with the script path as an argument, so between the kernel checking the script's permissions and the interpreter opening it there is a window in which an attacker can swap the file — a classic time-of-check-to-time-of-use race, made worse by the fact that the interpreter reopens the file by name. There is no clean fix, so `chmod u+s script.sh` simply has no effect on Linux.

The modern alternatives are much better. Capabilities split root's power into discrete privileges, so `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep` lets a binary bind port 443 without any other root power — this is why `ping` is no longer setuid-root but carries `cap_net_raw`. For services, systemd's `AmbientCapabilities=` grants a capability without touching the filesystem at all. And where a human genuinely needs escalation, `sudo` with a narrow rule gives you an audit trail that a setuid bit never will.

interviewQA.q: How would you find which process is listening on port 8080 and stop it safely?
interviewQA.a:
`ss -ltnp | grep :8080` — listening, TCP, numeric, with the owning process, and I need root to see the process column. `lsof -nP -i :8080` gives the same answer including the user and whether the socket is listening or established. `fuser -n tcp 8080` is a third option. I use `ss` rather than `netstat` because `netstat` walks `/proc/net` in a way that is very slow on a host with a lot of sockets, and it is not installed by default on modern distributions.

Then I find out *what* it is before killing anything: `ps -fp <pid>`, `readlink /proc/<pid>/exe` for the real binary, `/proc/<pid>/cwd`, and `systemctl status <pid>` — which is the important step, because if it is managed by systemd, killing the process directly will just make the supervisor restart it, and the right action is `systemctl stop`. In a container context the same logic applies with the runtime.

To stop it, SIGTERM first: `systemctl stop foo`, or `kill <pid>`, then confirm with `ss` that the socket has gone. If it does not exit within a sensible window I would find out *why* before escalating — a `D` state means it is blocked in the kernel and SIGKILL will not help either; a live process ignoring TERM might be mid-shutdown, draining connections. SIGKILL is the last resort, and I would note that it means no flush and no cleanup, so lock files and partial state may be left behind.

Two related things worth mentioning. If the port is bound but nothing seems to own it, check other network namespaces (`lsns -t net`, or `nsenter`) because a container has its own stack. And if the intent is to free the port for a new process, remember `TIME_WAIT` sockets on the *client* side do not block a listener, but a lingering listener with `SO_REUSEADDR` unset can produce "Address already in use" for a short window after a crash.

interviewQA.q: You get "No space left on device" but df -h shows 40% free. What is happening?
interviewQA.a:
The most likely cause is inode exhaustion. Every file, directory and symlink consumes one inode, and on ext2/3/4 the inode table is sized at `mkfs` time and cannot grow. A filesystem full of tiny files — PHP session files, an unpruned cache, mail spool, per-request log files, a runaway temp directory — can run out of inodes while blocks remain plentiful. The application sees `ENOSPC`, which is the same error as a full disk. `df -i` shows IUse% at 100% and confirms it instantly.

The fix is to delete files, and to delete them efficiently, because removing millions of small files is itself slow and I/O heavy: `find /path -xdev -type f -mtime +7 -delete` rather than `rm $(find ...)`, which would build an enormous argument list and can fail with "argument list too long". Then fix the root cause — add rotation, add a retention policy, or shard the directory, since a single directory with millions of entries is also a performance problem in its own right. Longer term, either reformat with a higher inode count (`mkfs.ext4 -N` or `-i`) or move to XFS, which allocates inodes dynamically.

There are a few other ways to get `ENOSPC` with apparently free space. On ext4, the reserved-blocks pool (5% by default, root-only) means non-root writes fail before `df` reads 100% — although `df`'s Use% column already accounts for that, so this shows as 100% rather than 40%. On a filesystem with quotas enabled, a user or group over quota gets `EDQUOT`, which some tools report loosely. `/dev/shm` or another tmpfs filling up looks like a full disk but is really RAM. On btrfs, metadata and data are allocated in separate chunks, so metadata can be exhausted while data space remains, which is a well-known confusing case. And a directory can hit ext4's own limits with an extremely large number of entries.

So my order of checks would be: `df -i`, then which filesystem the path is actually on (`df -hT /path`, since it may be a tmpfs or a different mount than assumed), then quotas (`repquota`), then the filesystem-specific cases.

interviewQA.q: Your process was OOM-killed. How do you confirm it, and what do you do about it?
interviewQA.a:
Confirmation first, because \"the process disappeared\" has several possible causes. The kernel logs every OOM kill, so `dmesg -T | grep -iE 'out of memory|oom-kill'` or `journalctl -k -b -g 'Out of memory'` gives a definitive line naming the victim, its PID, its `anon-rss` at the moment of death, and the cgroup it was in — plus a table of candidate processes and their scores. From the service side, `systemctl status` shows `killed, signal=KILL`, and in Kubernetes the container's last state is `OOMKilled` with exit code 137, which is 128+9. If there is no OOM line in the kernel log, it was something else — a crash, a SIGTERM from a deploy, or a liveness probe restart.

The next question is *which* OOM. A system-wide OOM means the whole machine ran out and the kernel picked the largest scorer, which is usually your main application even if it was not the process that leaked — that is worth saying, because the victim is frequently not the culprit. A cgroup OOM means the process exceeded its own `memory.max`, and the rest of the machine was fine; that is what a container memory limit produces, and `memory.events`'s `oom_kill` counter in the cgroup directory records it.

Then the actual work: is it a leak, a spike, or a limit that was always too low? I would look at the RSS trend over time in whatever metrics exist — steady growth to the ceiling implies a leak, a sawtooth implies GC pressure with a heap that is too large for the limit, and a sudden step implies a specific request pattern such as an unbounded query result or a large file loaded into memory. For a JVM I would check that heap plus metaspace plus thread stacks plus direct buffers actually fit inside the container limit, because setting `-Xmx` equal to the limit guarantees an eventual kill. I would also check for tmpfs usage, since files in `/dev/shm` count as memory and are not reclaimable.

Mitigations in order of preference: fix the leak or bound the workload (pagination, streaming instead of buffering, connection and queue limits); size the limit correctly with headroom over observed peak; set `MemoryHigh=` below `MemoryMax=` so the kernel throttles and reclaims before killing; use `OOMScoreAdjust`/`oom_score_adj` to make a critical process a less likely victim and a sacrificial one more likely; and make sure the process restarts cleanly and idempotently, because SIGKILL means it never got to flush anything.
