interviewQA.q: Give me a one-liner for the top 10 client IPs in an nginx access log, and explain each stage.
interviewQA.a:
`awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (ip in c) print c[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn | head -10`

`awk` reads the file line by line, splitting each on runs of whitespace, so `$1` is the client IP in the combined log format. `c[$1]++` uses an associative array keyed by IP as a counter — awk creates the entry on first use, so there is no initialisation. The `END` block runs once after the last line and prints each count with its key. Then `sort -rn` sorts numerically in reverse on the leading count field, and `head -10` takes the top ten. It is a single pass over the file with memory proportional to the number of distinct IPs, not to the file size, so it works on a multi-gigabyte log.

The alternative you often see is `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`. It gives the same answer but it sorts the entire dataset — every line — just so that `uniq` can collapse adjacent duplicates, which is far more expensive in CPU, memory and temporary disk space on a large file. It is worth being able to explain that difference, and to point out that `uniq` only ever collapses *adjacent* lines, which is why the first `sort` is mandatory in that version.

From there the same shape answers most log questions: swap `$1` for `$9` to count status codes, use `$7` for URL paths, add a condition like `$9 ~ /^5/` to restrict to server errors, or `split($4, t, ":"); c[t[2]":"t[3]]++` to get requests per minute. For percentiles I would extract the latency field, `sort -n`, and index at the position I need — although at that point, if this is a recurring need rather than an incident, the right answer is that these logs should be shipped to something that can query them, and one-liners are for the machine you are SSHed into at 3am.

interviewQA.q: What happens to a child process when its parent dies? And what exactly is a zombie?
interviewQA.a:
If the parent dies first, the child becomes an *orphan* and the kernel re-parents it to PID 1 — or, more precisely, to the nearest ancestor marked as a child subreaper via `prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER)`, which is how systemd user managers and container runtimes keep orphans inside their own supervision tree. The child keeps running; nothing about its execution changes. That re-parenting is what makes daemonisation by double-fork work, and it is also why a background job survives its parent shell unless it gets SIGHUP from the terminal going away.

A *zombie* is the opposite situation. When a process exits, the kernel frees its memory and file descriptors but must keep the exit status somewhere until the parent asks for it, because the parent has a right to know how its child ended. So a minimal task entry stays in the process table with state `Z`, shown by `ps` as `<defunct>`. It uses no memory and no CPU — it is already dead — but it holds a PID. When the parent calls `wait()`/`waitpid()`, the status is collected and the entry disappears. That is called reaping.

You cannot kill a zombie; signals are meaningless to a process that no longer runs. The bug is always in the parent: it forked children and never waited for them, usually because it ignored SIGCHLD without setting `SA_NOCLDWAIT`, or because its event loop never calls `wait`. The fix is to fix or restart the parent — when the parent dies, its zombies are re-parented to PID 1, which reaps immediately, and they vanish.

Why it matters in production: a few zombies are harmless, but a leaking supervisor accumulates them until the system hits `kernel.pid_max` or the cgroup's `pids.max`, and then *nothing* on the machine can fork — you cannot even run `ps` to diagnose it. The container-specific version of this is that a process running as PID 1 inherits init's duty of reaping orphans, and most application runtimes do not implement it, so a container that spawns subprocesses accumulates zombies. That is exactly what `tini` or `docker run --init` is for, alongside its signal-forwarding job.
followUps: How do you find the parent responsible for a pile of zombies?
Why does a container need an init process at all?
What is the double-fork daemonisation trick and why does it work?

interviewQA.q: You add a user to a group and they still get permission denied. Why?
interviewQA.a:
Group membership is resolved at login. The kernel stores the credentials — real and effective UID and GID plus the list of supplementary GIDs — in the process, and every child inherits them across `fork` and keeps them across `exec`. Editing `/etc/group` changes the *database*, not any process that is already running. So the user's existing shell, their SSH session, their tmux panes, and any daemon started before the change all keep the old group list until they are replaced.

The confirmation is that `id` inside the old shell still shows the old groups while `id <user>` run fresh (or `getent group <grp>`) shows the new membership. The fix is a new session: log out and back in, open a new SSH connection, or use `newgrp <group>` to spawn a subshell with the new group applied. For a service, restart the unit. This is exactly why "I added myself to the `docker` group but still get permission denied on the socket" is such a common first-day problem.

Two adjacent mistakes are worth flagging. `usermod -G` without `-a` *replaces* the entire supplementary group list, which is how people accidentally remove themselves from `sudo` and lock themselves out — it is always `usermod -aG`. And on a machine using LDAP or SSSD, group membership comes through NSS, so `grep` on `/etc/group` proves nothing; you must use `getent group`, and there may be a cache (`sss_cache -E` or restarting `sssd`) holding the old answer for minutes.

If a fresh login still fails, then it is not the group at all, and I would check whether the directory chain has the traverse bit for that group with `namei -l <path>`, whether an ACL or SELinux/AppArmor policy is denying it (`getfacl`, and `ausearch -m avc` on RHEL, since SELinux denials look exactly like permission errors), and whether the filesystem is mounted read-only or `nosuid`/`noexec`.

How would you check whether SELinux is what's denying you?

interviewQA.q: How do you rotate logs for an application that keeps its log file open, and why is that tricky?
interviewQA.a:
The difficulty is that a process holds a file descriptor to the *inode*, not to the name. `logrotate`'s default strategy renames `app.log` to `app.log.1` and creates a new empty `app.log`. The running application never notices — it keeps writing into the same inode, which is now called `app.log.1`, and after the next rotation gets compressed or deleted. New log lines effectively vanish, and if the old file was deleted while still open, the disk space is never reclaimed, which then shows up as `df` and `du` disagreeing.

There are two correct answers. The preferred one is `postrotate`: after renaming, signal the application to close and reopen its log files. nginx uses SIGUSR1 for exactly this, many daemons use SIGHUP, and systemd-managed services can be signalled with `systemctl kill -s HUP unit`. The application then opens the new file by name and picks up the fresh inode. The second option, for applications that cannot reopen, is `copytruncate`: logrotate copies the contents to the rotated name and then truncates the original file in place. Because the inode is preserved, the open descriptor stays valid. The costs are real — any lines written between the copy and the truncate are lost, and during the copy you need space for two copies of the file — so it is a fallback, not a default.

Beyond the mechanism, a few things I would make sure of. Set `create 0640 app adm` so the new file has the right owner and mode rather than inheriting whatever the rotating process's umask produced. Use `delaycompress` when combining with a reopen signal, so the most recent rotation is not compressed while the app might still be writing to it. Use `notifempty` and `missingok` to avoid noise. Test with `logrotate -d` (debug/dry-run) before shipping, because a broken rotation config is only discovered when a disk fills. And check `size` or `maxsize` as well as a time-based schedule, since a daily rotation is no help against a service that produces 50 GB in an hour.

The design-level answer is that under systemd or in containers the application should log to stdout/stderr and let journald or the container runtime handle collection and rotation entirely, which removes this whole class of problem — and that whatever the local arrangement, logs you actually depend on need to be shipped off the host.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through diagnosing "the server is slow" when you have SSH access and five minutes.
interviewQA.a:
I work resource by resource — CPU, memory, disk, network — and for each I look at utilisation, saturation and errors, because saturation is usually where the answer is and it is the part people skip.

I start with `uptime` for load average read against `nproc`, and compare the 1-, 5- and 15-minute figures to see whether it is arriving or receding. Then `dmesg -T | tail -30`, because OOM kills, filesystem errors, NIC resets and TCP memory exhaustion appear there and nowhere else, and finding one usually ends the investigation immediately.

Then `vmstat 1 5`, ignoring the first line since it is an average since boot. `r` is the run queue: consistently above core count means CPU saturation. `b` is processes blocked on I/O. `si`/`so` non-zero means the machine is actively swapping, which explains almost any latency problem on its own. Very high `cs` or `in` suggests a context-switch or interrupt storm. The CPU columns tell me where time is going: `us` means application code, `sy` means kernel, `wa` means waiting on storage, `si` means softirq which is usually network, and `st` means steal — the hypervisor giving my CPU to another tenant, which is an instance problem, not a code problem.

Branching from there: if it is CPU, `mpstat -P ALL 1` distinguishes one hot core (single-threaded bottleneck, or interrupts pinned to CPU0) from an evenly loaded box, and `pidstat 1` or `top -o %CPU` names the process. If it is I/O, `iostat -xz 1` gives me `await` — the latency the application actually feels — and `aqu-sz` for queue depth, with the caveat that `%util` is misleading on NVMe because it serves requests in parallel; `pidstat -d 1` attributes I/O to processes. If it is memory, `free -h` looking at *available* rather than free, plus the swap rate from vmstat. If it is network, `ss -s` for socket counts, `ss -ltn` where a non-zero Recv-Q on a listening socket means the application is not accepting fast enough, and `nstat` for retransmits and listen-queue overflows.

`/proc/pressure/{cpu,io,memory}` is the fastest single saturation signal if the kernel supports it — `some avg10` is the percentage of the last ten seconds during which at least one task was stalled on that resource.

Then I narrow to the process: `strace -c -p <pid>` for a syscall profile (with the caveat that it slows the target substantially), `perf top` for where CPU time is being spent, and `/proc/<pid>/wchan` or `stack` for anything stuck in `D` state. And throughout I would be asking what changed — a deploy, a config change, a traffic shift, a dependency getting slower — because the answer is far more often a change than a spontaneous hardware event.
followUps: You find high wa and iostat shows 40ms await. What next?
Steal time is 25%. What do you tell the team?
Everything looks idle but latency is bad. Where do you look?
Why is the first line of vmstat and iostat output misleading?

interviewQA.q: How would you limit the CPU and memory a service can use, without containers?
interviewQA.a:
With cgroups, which is exactly what containers use anyway — and on a systemd host the ergonomic way in is unit directives, because every service already runs in its own cgroup.

In the unit's `[Service]` section: `MemoryMax=2G` is a hard limit, and exceeding it triggers a cgroup OOM kill of a process inside that cgroup only, leaving the rest of the machine alone. `MemoryHigh=1500M` is a throttle rather than a wall — past it the kernel reclaims aggressively and stalls the cgroup, which is often better than a kill because it degrades instead of dying. `CPUQuota=150%` means 1.5 cores' worth of CPU time per period, implemented as the cgroup's `cpu.max` bandwidth control. `CPUWeight=` sets relative priority under contention rather than a cap. `TasksMax=` bounds process and thread count, which is real fork-bomb protection. `IOWeight=` and `IOReadBandwidthMax=` cover block I/O on cgroup v2 with the right controllers enabled. `LimitNOFILE=` and friends set classic per-process rlimits, which are a different mechanism — rlimits are per process, cgroup limits are for the whole group collectively.

For an ad-hoc command, `systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=1G -p CPUQuota=50% -- ./import.sh` puts a one-off job under the same controls without writing a unit file, which is genuinely useful for a risky migration or backfill. Underneath, all of this is just writing to `/sys/fs/cgroup/...`: `memory.max`, `cpu.max`, `pids.max` in the unified v2 hierarchy, and you can read `memory.current`, `cpu.stat` and `memory.events` back for accounting. `systemd-cgtop` shows live usage per unit and slice.

Two design points I would add. Slices let you group services and cap them collectively — you can put all batch work in a slice with a CPU weight so it can never starve interactive services. And the choice between a throttle and a hard cap matters: for latency-sensitive services I prefer `MemoryHigh` plus alerting, so I get reclaim pressure and a warning rather than a surprise SIGKILL, and I reserve `MemoryMax` as the backstop that protects the machine.

Worth saying explicitly: `nice` and `ionice` are not equivalents. They adjust scheduling priority within the CPU and I/O schedulers, they are advisory and relative, and they cannot bound absolute consumption. cgroups can.

How is this different from nice and ulimit?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between a login shell, a non-login interactive shell, and a non-interactive shell, and why does it matter operationally?
interviewQA.a:
They differ in which startup files bash reads, and that determines what environment your commands actually run in.

A *login* shell — what you get from an SSH session, a console login, or `bash -l`, `su -`, `sudo -i` — reads `/etc/profile` and then the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login` or `~/.profile` that exists. A *non-login interactive* shell — a new terminal tab in a desktop session, or `bash` typed at a prompt, or a tmux pane depending on configuration — reads `/etc/bash.bashrc` and `~/.bashrc` instead. That is why the common idiom is for `~/.bash_profile` to source `~/.bashrc`, so you get one consistent environment either way. A *non-interactive* shell — a script with a shebang, a command run over `ssh host 'cmd'`, or a cron job — reads *neither*; bash only sources the file named by `$BASH_ENV` if that variable is set, which normally it is not.

Operationally this explains an entire family of "works for me" bugs. A cron job cannot find a binary because `~/.bashrc` set the `PATH` and cron never read it. `ssh host 'mycommand'` fails while logging in and typing the same thing works, because the first is non-interactive and the second is a login shell. A systemd service does not see an environment variable that is set in every developer's terminal, because systemd sources no shell files at all — variables must come from `Environment=` or `EnvironmentFile=`. A Docker `RUN` step behaves differently from an interactive `docker exec` shell for the same reason.

There is one more trap: many distributions put an early return in `~/.bashrc` guarded by `case $- in *i*) ;; *) return;; esac`, so even if something does source it non-interactively, the interesting parts are skipped.

The discipline that follows is: never rely on shell startup files for anything a machine depends on. Put environment for services in the unit file or an `EnvironmentFile`, put environment for cron jobs explicitly in the crontab or inside the script, use absolute paths in automation, and treat `~/.bashrc` as strictly a human convenience. If you need to reproduce a failure, `env -i` gives you an empty environment so you can add things back one at a time and find out what the script was silently depending on.

flashcards.front: What does an inode contain, and what does it NOT contain?
flashcards.back: It contains file type, permission bits, owner UID/GID, size, timestamps, link count, and pointers to the data blocks. It does NOT contain the filename - names live in directory entries as (name, inode number) pairs.

flashcards.front: Hard link vs symlink in one sentence each
flashcards.back: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode (same filesystem only, no directories, link count +1). A symlink is a separate inode whose content is a path string, resolved on every access - crosses filesystems, breaks silently if the target moves.

flashcards.front: Why can df show a full disk while du shows half of it used?
flashcards.back: Deleted-but-still-open files (space held until the last fd closes), files hidden under a mount point, ext4's 5% root-reserved blocks, or sparse/hard-linked files that du undercounts. Check `lsof +L1` first.

flashcards.front: Two ways to reclaim space from a deleted-but-open log file
flashcards.back: Make the process reopen its logs (SIGUSR1 for nginx, SIGHUP for many daemons, or restart the service), or truncate through the descriptor: `truncate -s 0 /proc/<pid>/fd/<n>`.

flashcards.front: `No space left on device` but `df -h` shows plenty free. First check?
flashcards.back: `df -i` - inode exhaustion. ext4 fixes the inode count at mkfs time, so millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while blocks remain. XFS allocates inodes dynamically.

flashcards.front: What does the execute bit mean on a directory?
flashcards.back: Traverse/search: you may resolve a path through it to reach entries inside. You need x on every directory in a path. Without r you cannot list the names, but with x alone you can still open a file whose exact name you know.

flashcards.front: Which permission lets you delete a file?
flashcards.back: Write permission on the containing DIRECTORY, not on the file. That is why you can delete a file you cannot read, and why /tmp needs the sticky bit.

flashcards.front: umask 027 - what mode do a new file and a new directory get?
flashcards.back: File 0640 (0666 & ~027), directory 0750 (0777 & ~027). Files never get the execute bit at creation. umask is a per-process attribute inherited across fork.

flashcards.front: What do setuid, setgid and the sticky bit do?
flashcards.back: setuid (4000): run with the file owner's effective UID. setgid (2000): run with the file's group, or on a DIRECTORY make new entries inherit that group. Sticky (1000) on a directory: only the owner may delete or rename an entry (/tmp is 1777).

flashcards.front: Why is setuid ignored on shell scripts on Linux?
flashcards.back: Executing a script means the kernel runs the interpreter, which then re-opens the script by name - an unfixable time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. So `chmod u+s script.sh` has no effect.

flashcards.front: How do you let a non-root process bind to port 443?
flashcards.back: Grant CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE - `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /path/bin`, or `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` in the systemd unit. Alternatives: high port plus a firewall redirect, or a reverse proxy.

flashcards.front: Why does Unix split process creation into fork() and exec()?
flashcards.back: So the child can be configured in the gap between them: dup2 for redirection, setuid to drop privileges, chdir, rlimits, closing descriptors. A single atomic spawn call would need every one of those as a parameter.

flashcards.front: What is a zombie process and how do you get rid of it?
flashcards.back: A process that has exited whose parent has not called wait() to collect the exit status. It holds a PID but no memory or CPU and cannot be killed - it is already dead. Fix or restart the PARENT; its zombies are then re-parented to PID 1, which reaps them.

flashcards.front: What happens to a child when its parent dies?
flashcards.back: It is re-parented to PID 1, or to the nearest ancestor registered as a child subreaper via prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER). It keeps running normally.

flashcards.front: Why can't you kill a process in D state?
flashcards.back: D is uninterruptible sleep inside a kernel I/O path. The process does not return to userspace to handle any signal - not even SIGKILL - until that I/O completes or errors. Typical cause: a hung NFS mount or a failing disk.

flashcards.front: SIGTERM vs SIGKILL
flashcards.back: SIGTERM (15) is catchable: the app can drain connections, flush, and exit cleanly. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught, blocked or ignored - the kernel removes the process with no cleanup, so buffers, temp files and locks are left behind.
128+N means killed by signal N: 130 = SIGINT (Ctrl-C), 137 = SIGKILL (in k8s usually OOMKilled), 143 = SIGTERM (normal orchestrated stop). 126 = found but not executable, 127 = command not found.

flashcards.front: Why does a containerised app ignore `docker stop`?
flashcards.back: The kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1 for signals it has not explicitly handled, so an app with no SIGTERM handler ignores it and gets SIGKILLed after the grace period. Also, shell-form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1 and it does not forward signals. Fix: exec form, `exec "$@"` in the entrypoint, or `--init`/tini.

flashcards.front: Requires= vs After= in systemd
flashcards.back: Requires= is a requirement (pull the unit in; fail/stop with it). After= is ordering only. Neither implies the other - Requires= without After= lets both start simultaneously and race. Wants= is the soft, non-failing form of Requires=.

flashcards.front: What do systemd Type=simple, forking, oneshot and notify mean?
flashcards.back: simple: considered started as soon as the process is forked (default). forking: the daemon backgrounds itself; needs PIDFile=. oneshot: runs and exits, usually with RemainAfterExit=yes. notify: the service calls sd_notify(READY=1) when genuinely ready - the only one where ordering means readiness.

flashcards.front: "Start request repeated too quickly" - what happened?
flashcards.back: The unit exceeded StartLimitBurst starts (default 5) within StartLimitIntervalSec (default 10s), so systemd latched it into failed state and stopped restarting it. Fix the cause, then `systemctl reset-failed <unit>`.

flashcards.front: How do you override a vendor systemd unit safely?
flashcards.back: `systemctl edit <unit>` writes a drop-in at /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/override.conf, which survives package upgrades. List directives such as ExecStart= append, so clear them first with an empty assignment. Then `systemctl daemon-reload`; verify with `systemctl cat`.

flashcards.front: cron: if both day-of-month and day-of-week are set, when does the job run?
flashcards.back: When EITHER matches - the two fields are OR'ed, not AND'ed. `0 0 13 * 5` runs on every Friday AND on the 13th.

flashcards.front: Why does a cron job fail when the same command works in your shell?
flashcards.back: cron sources no shell startup files: minimal PATH (typically /usr/bin:/bin), SHELL=/bin/sh, no JAVA_HOME/virtualenv/AWS_PROFILE, no TTY, cwd = $HOME. Also, an unescaped % in a crontab becomes a newline. Use absolute paths and set PATH explicitly.

flashcards.front: Three things a systemd timer gives you that cron does not
flashcards.back: Persistent=true catches up runs missed while the machine was down; RandomizedDelaySec= spreads a fleet out; and the job is a real unit, so it has journal logs, exit status, resource limits and sandboxing. Note timers default to AccuracySec=1min.

flashcards.front: dpkg vs apt (and rpm vs dnf)
flashcards.back: dpkg/rpm are the low layer: install, remove and query a package file already on disk, with no dependency resolution. apt/dnf are the high layer: talk to signed repositories, resolve the dependency graph, download in order, and hand files to the low layer.

flashcards.front: Which package owns /usr/sbin/nginx, and which files does the nginx package own?
flashcards.back: `dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx` and `dpkg -L nginx` on Debian/Ubuntu; `rpm -qf /usr/sbin/nginx` and `rpm -ql nginx` on RHEL. `rpm -V nginx` additionally verifies installed files against the package database.

flashcards.front: Why is patching not finished when the package manager exits?
flashcards.back: Upgrading a shared library does not restart processes that already mapped the old one - they keep running the vulnerable code and hold `(deleted)` .so files. Use `needrestart` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `dnf needs-restarting -r` (RHEL) to find what still needs restarting or a reboot.

flashcards.front: journalctl flags worth memorising
flashcards.back: -u UNIT, -f follow, -n N last lines, -b this boot / -b -1 previous boot, -k kernel, -p err priority, --since/--until, -o json, -g PATTERN grep, --disk-usage, --vacuum-time=7d.

flashcards.front: Why did the journal disappear after a reboot?
flashcards.back: Storage was volatile - the journal was in /run/log/journal (tmpfs). Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and ensure /var/log/journal exists. Size is bounded by SystemMaxUse=, defaulting to 10% of the filesystem capped at 4 GiB.

flashcards.front: Why can logrotate make an app's log lines disappear?
flashcards.back: The app holds a descriptor to the INODE, not the name, so after a rename it keeps writing into the rotated (then compressed or deleted) file. Fix with a postrotate signal telling the app to reopen (SIGUSR1 for nginx, HUP for many daemons), or use copytruncate if it cannot.

flashcards.front: What does copytruncate cost you?
flashcards.back: Any lines written between the copy and the truncate are lost, and you briefly need disk space for two copies. Use it only when the application cannot be told to reopen its log files.

flashcards.front: Why use `getent passwd alice` instead of grepping /etc/passwd?
flashcards.back: getent goes through NSS, so it also resolves users from LDAP, SSSD or another directory - which is where the accounts actually live on a domain-joined host. grep only sees local files.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't adding a user to a group take effect immediately?
flashcards.back: Group membership is baked into a process's credentials at login and inherited by children. Existing shells and running services keep the old list. Log out and back in, use `newgrp <group>`, or restart the service. Also: always `usermod -aG` - without -a you REPLACE the group list.

flashcards.front: Which sudo grants are secretly full root?
flashcards.back: Any command that can spawn a shell or write arbitrary files: vi/vim (:!sh), less, find (-exec), awk (system()), tar/rsync with checkpoint or -e options, chmod, and most wildcard rules. Prefer sudoedit and narrow purpose-built wrapper scripts.

flashcards.front: What crosses the wire during SSH public key auth?
flashcards.back: The client's PUBLIC key and a signature over data that includes the session identifier. The private key never leaves the client, and because the signature is bound to that session it cannot be replayed on another connection.

flashcards.front: SSH key auth silently falls back to a password prompt. First thing to check?
flashcards.back: Permissions - sshd's StrictModes rejects authorized_keys if ~, ~/.ssh or the file itself is group- or world-writable. Want ~ 755 or tighter, ~/.ssh 700, authorized_keys 600, all owned by the user. On SELinux hosts also run `restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh`. Then `ssh -vvv` plus `journalctl -u ssh`.

flashcards.front: Why prefer ProxyJump over agent forwarding?
flashcards.back: Agent forwarding exposes your agent socket on the remote host, so root there can authenticate as you anywhere your keys are trusted. ProxyJump (`ssh -J bastion`) tunnels the connection through the bastion while the signing stays on your laptop.

flashcards.front: Why must you use `find -print0 | xargs -0`?
flashcards.back: Plain xargs splits on whitespace and interprets quotes, so a filename containing a space or newline becomes several arguments. NUL is the one byte that cannot appear in a filename. Add GNU `xargs -r` so an empty input does not run the command at all.

flashcards.front: `-exec cmd {} \;` vs `-exec cmd {} +`
flashcards.back: `\;` runs the command once per file; `+` batches as many files per invocation as fit on a command line, like xargs. For large trees `+` is dramatically faster - use it unless the command genuinely takes one file at a time.

flashcards.front: What does `find -mtime +7` actually mean?
flashcards.back: Modification age in 24-hour units, truncated, greater than 7 - i.e. at least 8 days ago. `-mtime 0` means within the last 24 hours. Use -mmin for minute granularity, and always add -xdev to stay on one filesystem.

flashcards.front: awk one-liner: top 10 client IPs in an access log
flashcards.back: `awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (i in c) print c[i], i}' access.log | sort -rn | head -10`. One pass, memory proportional to distinct IPs - much cheaper than `sort | uniq -c`, which sorts every line first.

flashcards.front: Why does `sort -k2` not sort on field 2?
flashcards.back: A -k with no end field means "from field 2 to the end of the line". Write -k2,2 for field 2 alone. Also `LC_ALL=C sort` is faster and gives stable byte ordering instead of locale-dependent collation.

flashcards.front: `cmd > out 2>&1` vs `cmd 2>&1 > out`
flashcards.back: Redirections apply left to right. The first sends stdout to the file, then stderr to wherever stdout now points - both to the file. The second points stderr at the terminal (stdout's current target), then moves stdout to the file - so errors still hit the terminal.

flashcards.front: Why does `false | true` exit 0, and how do you fix it?
flashcards.back: A pipeline's status is that of its LAST command. `set -o pipefail` makes it the rightmost non-zero status instead, and bash's PIPESTATUS array holds every stage's status individually.

flashcards.front: Why does `tail -f log | grep ERROR` appear to hang?
flashcards.back: C stdio block-buffers when stdout is a pipe instead of line-buffering to a terminal, so grep holds matches until its buffer fills. Fix with `grep --line-buffered`, `sed -u`, awk's fflush(), or `stdbuf -oL` on the producer.

flashcards.front: Why is `count` still 0 after `find ... | while read f; do count=$((count+1)); done`?
flashcards.back: Each stage of a bash pipeline runs in a subshell, so the variable is lost when the loop ends. Use process substitution: `while read f; do ...; done < <(find ...)`, or `shopt -s lastpipe`.

flashcards.front: Where does `set -e` NOT fire?
flashcards.back: Anywhere the status is being tested: inside if/while conditions, left of && or ||, after !, and inside any function called in those contexts. Worst case: `local x=$(cmd)` reports `local`'s status, hiding the failure - always split into `local x; x=$(cmd)`.

flashcards.front: Which column of `free -h` actually matters?
flashcards.back: `available` - the kernel's estimate of what a new workload could get without swapping, counting reclaimable page cache and slab. `free` is near zero on any healthy machine because unused RAM is used as page cache. Note `shared` (tmpfs) is NOT reclaimable.

flashcards.front: RSS vs VSZ vs PSS
flashcards.back: VSZ is reserved address space, including mapped files and untouched allocations - nearly meaningless as pressure. RSS is pages resident in RAM but counts shared pages in full against every process. PSS (/proc/PID/smaps_rollup) divides shared pages among sharers and is the honest number.

flashcards.front: How do you confirm a process was OOM-killed?
flashcards.back: `dmesg -T | grep -i 'out of memory'` or `journalctl -k -g 'Out of memory'` - the kernel logs the victim, its anon-rss and its cgroup. The process dies by SIGKILL, so exit status is 137. In Kubernetes that surfaces as OOMKilled.

flashcards.front: MemoryHigh vs MemoryMax
flashcards.back: MemoryHigh is a throttle: past it the kernel reclaims hard and stalls the cgroup, degrading rather than dying. MemoryMax is a hard wall: exceeding it triggers a cgroup OOM kill inside that cgroup only. Set High below Max so you get pressure and alerts before a SIGKILL.

flashcards.front: What does Linux load average actually count?
flashcards.back: An exponentially damped average (1/5/15 min) of tasks that are runnable OR in uninterruptible sleep (D state, i.e. blocked in kernel I/O). Including D state is why load can be 40 with a 90% idle CPU. Always read it against nproc.

flashcards.front: What does steal time (`st` in top) mean?
flashcards.back: CPU time the hypervisor gave to another tenant while your vCPU was runnable. Sustained non-zero steal on a cloud VM means the host is oversubscribed - the fix is a different instance type or host, not your code.

flashcards.front: In `iostat -xz 1`, which fields matter and which one lies?
flashcards.back: `await` (average latency in ms) is what the application feels, and `aqu-sz` is the saturation signal. `%util` means "time with at least one request in flight" - a valid proxy for one spinning disk, but misleading on SSD/NVMe, which serve many requests in parallel.

flashcards.front: Why ignore the first report from vmstat, iostat and sar?
flashcards.back: The first sample is an average since boot, not an instantaneous rate. Always take the second and later samples.

flashcards.front: What does a non-zero Recv-Q on a LISTENING socket mean?
flashcards.back: It is the number of completed connections waiting to be accept()ed; Send-Q is the configured backlog maximum. Non-zero Recv-Q means the application is not accepting fast enough, and clients are about to see failures. Confirm with `nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows`.

flashcards.front: Fastest way to see what a stuck process is waiting on
flashcards.back: `cat /proc/<pid>/wchan` or `/proc/<pid>/stack` for the kernel function it is blocked in, `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` for open files and sockets, `/proc/<pid>/status` for threads and memory. `strace -f -p <pid>` if you can afford the slowdown.

flashcards.front: What is /proc/pressure and why is it useful?
flashcards.back: Pressure Stall Information: for cpu, io and memory, `some avg10` is the percentage of the last 10 seconds during which at least one task was stalled waiting for that resource. It is the kernel's most direct saturation metric, and it exists per cgroup too.

flashcards.front: Which shell startup files does a non-interactive shell read?
flashcards.back: None. Scripts, `ssh host 'cmd'` and cron jobs read neither /etc/profile nor ~/.bashrc (only $BASH_ENV if set). That is why automation must use absolute paths and set its environment explicitly - and why systemd services need Environment= or EnvironmentFile=.

flashcards.front: How do you stop two runs of a script overlapping?
flashcards.back: `exec 9>/run/lock/job.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 0` at the top - the lock is released automatically when the process exits and fd 9 closes. Under systemd you get this for free: a unit only runs one instance at a time.

flashcards.front: How do you publish a config file so readers never see a partial write?
flashcards.back: Write to a temporary file in the SAME filesystem, then `mv` it over the target. rename(2) is atomic within a filesystem, so every reader sees either the whole old file or the whole new one. Pair it with `trap cleanup EXIT` and `mktemp -d`.
